But the CHURCH OF GOD, the city on a hill (Isa. ii. 2; Gal. iv. 26), in allusion to their present situation, on a mountain, is most probably the leading thought.
5:15: 15. μόδιον] A Latin word, called by the more general name σκεῦος, Luke viii. 16. καίουσιν, i.e. men in general: shewing, in the spiritual reference of the parable, that these lights of the world are 'lighted' by Him for whose use they are.
5:16:
16. οὕτως] i.e. like a candle on a candlestick — like a city on a hill; not οὕτως, ὅπως, 'so that,' as our English version seems rather to imply.

The sense of this verse is as if it were ὅπως, ἰδόντες ὑμῶν τ. κ. ἔργ. δοξάσωσιν τ. π. ὑ. — the latter verb, and not the former, carrying the purpose of the action. Thus the praise and glory of a well-lighted and brilliant feast would be given, not to the lights, but to the master of the house. The whole of this division of our Lord's sermon is addressed to all His followers, not exclusively to the ministers of his word. All servants of Christ are the salt of the earth, the light of the world (Phil. ii. 15). But à fortiori does it apply, in its highest sense, to those who are, among Christians, selected to teach and be examples; who are as it were the towers and pinnacles of the city, not only not hid, but seen far and wide above the rest.
5:17:
vv. 17–48. The Second Part of the Sermon, in which our Lord sets forth His relation, as a lawgiver, to the law of Moses. 17. ἦλθον] Observe how our Lord, through the whole sermon, sets forth Himself, in his proceeding forth from God, as the true ἐρχόμενος.

τὸν ν. ἢ τοὺς προφ.] It is a question whether our Lord includes the prophecies, properly so called, in His meaning here. I think not: for no person professing himself to be the Messiah would be thought to contradict the prophecies, but to fulfil them. Neither, it appears, does He here allude to the sacrificial and typical parts of the law, but to the moral parts of both the law and the prophets; which indeed he proceeds to cite and particularize. 'Hæc praecepta sunt morum; illa sacramenta sunt promissorum: hæc implentur per adjuvantem gratiam, illa per redditam veritatem, utraque per Christum' (Augustine, Contra Faust. xix. 18).

πληρῶσαι implies more than the mere fulfilling: i.e. here, giving a deeper and holier sense to — fulfilling in the spirit, which is nobler than the letter. Theophylact compares the ancient law to a sketch, which the painter οὐ καταλύει, ἀλλ᾽ ἀναπληροῖ.
5:18:
18. ἀμήν, ἀληθῶς, in St. Luke. The double ἕως ἄν renders the dependence of the members of the sentence rather difficult. According to one view these latter words will mean, 'till the end of all things.' But the other interpretation, 'till all (that is written in the law) shall have been fulfilled' (as in the English version), is no doubt admissible: while heaven and earth last (ἕως ἂν ὁ κόσμος διαμένῃ, Euthymius) one jot or one tittle shall not pass away from the law without all being fulfilled.

ἰῶτα is the Hebrew Jod, the smallest letter in the alphabet: κεραῖαι are the little turns of the strokes by which one letter differs from another similar to it. Origen on Ps. xxxiii. says — τῶν στοιχείων παρ᾽ Ἑβραίοις, λέγω δὲ τοῦ χὰρ καὶ τοῦ βήθ πολλὴν ὁμοιότητα σωζόντων, ὡς κατὰ μηδὲν ἀλλήλων διαλλάττειν ἢ βραχείᾳ κεραίᾳ μόνῃ.

It is important to observe in these days how the Lord here includes the O.T. and all its unfolding of the divine purposes regarding Himself, in His teaching of the citizens of the kingdom of heaven. I say this, because it is always in contempt and setting aside of the O.T. that rationalism has begun. First, its historical truth — then its theocratic dispensation and the types and prophecies connected with it, are swept away; so that Christ came to fulfil nothing, and becomes only a teacher or a martyr: and thus the way is paved for a similar rejection of the N.T. — beginning with the narratives of the birth and infancy, as theocratic myths — advancing to the denial of His miracles — then attacking the truthfulness of His own sayings — and so finally leaving us nothing in the Scriptures but, as a German writer of this school has expressed it, 'a mythology not so attractive as that of Greece.' It should be a maxim for every expositor and every student, that Scripture is a whole, and stands or falls together. (Since these words were first written, we have had lamentable proof in England, that their warnings were not unneeded. The course of unbelief which induced the publication of the volume entitled 'Essays and Reviews,' was, in character and progress, exactly that above described.)
5:19: 19. There is little difficulty in this verse, if we consider it in connexion with the verse preceding, to which it is bound by the οὖν and the τούτων, and with the following, to which the γάρ unites it. Bearing this in mind, we see (1) that λύσῃ, on account of what follows in ver. 20 and after, must be taken in the higher sense, as referring to the spirit and not the letter; (2) that τῶν ἐντ. τούτ. τῶν ἐλ. refers to ἰῶτα ἓν ἢ μία κεραία above, and means one of those minute commands which seem as insignificant, in comparison with the greater, as the ἰῶτα and κεραία in comparison with great portions of writing; (3) that ἐλάχιστος κληθ. does not mean 'shall be excluded from,' inasmuch as the question is not of keeping or not keeping the commandments of God in a legal sense, but of appreciating, and causing others to appreciate, the import and weight of even the most insignificant parts of God's revelation of Himself to man; (4) that no deduction can be drawn from these words binding the Jewish law, or any part of it, as such, upon Christians; (5) that these words of our Lord are decisive against such persons, whether ancient or modern, as would set aside the Old Testament as without significance, or inconsistent with the New.
5:20:
20. An expansion of the idea contained in πληρῶσαι, ver. 17, and of the difference between λύσῃ, which the Scribes and Pharisees did by enforcing the letter to the neglect of the spirit — and ποιήσῃ καὶ διδάξῃ, in which particulars Christians were to exceed the Pharisees, the punctilious observers, and the Scribes, the traditional expounders of the law.

γραμματέων] Persons devoted to the work of reading and expounding the law, whose office seems first to have become frequent after the return from Babylon. They generally appear in the N.T. in connexion with the Pharisees. The Scribes uniformly opposed themselves to our Lord; watching Him to find matter of accusation, Luke vi. 7; xi. 53, 54; perverting His sayings, Matt. ix. 3, and His actions, Luke v. 30; xv. 2; seeking to entangle Him by questions, Matt. xxii. 35. Their authority as expounders of the law is recognized by our Lord Himself, Matt. xxiii. 1, 2.
5:21:
vv. 21–48. Six examples of the true fulfilment of the law by Jesus. First example. The law of murder. 21. ἠκούσατε] viz. by the reading of the law in the synagogues, and the exposition of the Scribes.

τοῖς ἀρχαίοις] has been rendered, as in E.V., 'by the ancients'; or, 'to the ancients' — which last interpretation seems to me to be certainly the right one. Chrysostom expands it thus: τί οὖν αὐτός φησιν; ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη τοῖς ἀρχαίοις Οὐ φονεύσεις· καίτοι ὁ καὶ ἐκεῖνα δοὺς αὐτός ἐστιν. It will be noticed that our Lord does not here speak against the abuse of the law by tradition, but that every instance here given is either from the law itself, or such traditional teaching as was in accordance with it. The contrasts here are not between the law misunderstood and the law rightly understood, but between the law and its ancient exposition — not between two lawgivers, Moses and Christ, but between οἱ ἀρχαῖοι and ὑμεῖς; between (the idea is Chrysostom's) the children, by the same husband, of the bondwoman and of the freewoman.
5:22:
22. The sense is: There were among the Jews three well-known degrees of guilt, coming respectively under the cognizance of the local and the supreme courts; and after these is set the γέεννα τοῦ πυρός, the end of the malefactor, whose corpse, thrown out into the valley of Hinnom, was devoured by the worm or the flame. Similarly, in the spiritual kingdom of Christ, shall the sins even of thought and word be brought into judgment and punished, each according to its degree of guilt, but even the least of them before no less a tribunal than the judgment-seat of Christ. The most important thing to keep in mind is, that there is no distinction of kind between these punishments, only of degree. So that the distinction drawn by the Romanists between venial and mortal sins, finds not only no countenance, but direct confutation from this passage.

ῥακά, empty; a term denoting contempt. μωρέ — two interpretations have been given: either (1) as usually understood, a Greek word, 'Thou fool,' used by our Lord Himself of the Scribes and Pharisees, ch. xxiii. 17, 19; or (2) a Hebrew word, signifying 'rebel,' the very word for uttering which Moses and Aaron were debarred from entering the land of promise, Num. xx. 10.

τ. γέενναν τοῦ π.] To the S.E. of Jerusalem was a deep and fertile valley, called the vale of Hinnom, rendered Γέεννα, Josh. xviii. 16, LXX. In this valley (also called Tophet) did the idolatrous Jews burn their children to Moloch, and Josiah (2 Kings xxiii. 10) therefore polluted it; and thenceforward it was the place for the casting out and burning all offal, and the corpses of criminals; and therefore its name, ἡ γέεννα τοῦ πυρός, was used to signify the place of everlasting punishment.
5:23:
23 f. οὖν] an inference from the guilt and danger of all bitterness and hostility of mind towards another, declared in the preceding verse. καθάπερ σοφὸς ἰατρὸς οὐ μόνον τὰ προφυλακτικὰ τῶν νοσημάτων τίθησιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ διορθωτικά, οὕτω καὶ αὐτὸς ποιεῖ (Chrysostom). The δῶρον is any kind of gift — sacrificial or eucharistic. ἔχει τὶ κατὰ σοῦ is remarkable, as being purposely substituted for the converse. It is not what complaints we have against others that we are to consider at such a time, but what they have against us.

Our διαλλάγηθι is simply 'become reconciled thyself,' without being influenced by the status of the other towards thee. πρῶτον belongs to ὕπαγε, not to διαλλάγηθι. No conclusion whatever can be drawn from this verse as to the admissibility of the term 'altar' as applied to the Lord's Table under the Christian system. The whole language is Jewish, and can only be understood of Jewish rites.
5:25: 25. The whole of this verse is the earthly example of a spiritual duty which is understood, and runs parallel with it. The sense may be given: 'As in worldly affairs, it is prudent to make up a matter with an adversary before judgment is passed, which may deliver a man to a hard and rigorous imprisonment, so reconciliation with an offended brother in this life is absolutely necessary before his wrong cry against us to the Great Judge, and we be cast into eternal condemnation.' The ἀντίδικος, in its abstract personification, is the offended law of God, which will cry against us in that day for all wrongs done to others; but in its concrete representation it is the offended brother, who is to us that law, as long as he has its claim upon us. The ὁδός, in the interpretation, is the way in which all men walk.
5:26:
26. These words, which in the earthly example imply future liberation, because an earthly debt can be paid in most cases, so in the spiritual counterpart amount to a negation of it, because the debt can never be discharged. We have ἕως ἀποδῷ τὸ ὀφειλόμενον in ch. xviii. 30, where the payment was clearly impossible.

ὑπηρέτης = πράκτωρ in Luke xii. 58, and is the officer of the court who saw the sentences executed. κοδράντην, quadrantem, a Latin word, the fourth part of an as.
5:27:
vv. 27–30. Second example. The law of adultery. 28. πᾶς ὁ βλέπων] The precise meaning should in this verse be kept in mind, as the neglect of it may lead into error. Our Lord is speaking of the sin of adultery, and therefore, however the saying may undoubtedly apply by implication to cases where this sin is out of the question, yet the direct assertion in this verse must be understood as applying to the cases where this sin is in question. And the βλέπων πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθ. must not be interpreted of the casual evil thought which is checked by holy watchfulness, but the gazing with a view to feed that desire. And ἤδη ἐμ. αὐτ. ἐν τῇ κ. αὐτ. affirms that the man who can do this has already in his heart passed the barrier of criminal intention.

But perhaps there is justice in Stier's remark, that our Lord speaks here after the O.T. usage, in which, both in the seventh commandment and elsewhere, adultery also includes fornication; for marriage is the becoming one flesh, and therefore every such union, except that after the manner and in the state appointed by God, is a violation and contempt of that holy ordinance.
5:29: 29. An admonition, arising out of the truth announced in the last verse, to withstand the first springs and occasions of evil desire, even by the sacrifice of what is most useful and dear to us. οὐ γὰρ ὁ ὀφθαλμός ἐστιν ὁ ὁρῶν, ἀλλ᾽ ὁ νοῦς καὶ ὁ λογισμός (Chrysostom). Euthymius adds that our Lord calls a right eye a friend dear as the eye, and a right hand a useful servant dear as the hand, whether man or woman, and bids us not spare even these if they cause us to stumble. Philo Judæus reports a similar interpretation of Deut. xxv. 12, that the precept is symbolical, not for the mutilation of the body, but to cut off all godless reasonings of the soul.
5:30: See note on ver. 29. We may observe here, that our Lord grounds His precept of the most rigid and decisive self-denial on the considerations of the truest self-interest, συμφέρει σοι. ἵνα belongs to συμφ. σοι, and not (Meyer) to the foregoing, making συμφ. γάρ σοι parenthetical.
5:31: vv. 31, 32. Third example. The law of divorce. See note on ch. xix. 7–9. Lightfoot gives a form of the ἀποστάσιον, which was a divorcement a vinculo matrimonii, and placed the woman absolutely in her own power, to marry whom she pleased, unless the husband inserted a special clause to bar this. In Deut. xxiv. 1, the allowable reason of divorce is 'some uncleanness.' This the disciples of Shammai interpreted only of adultery; those of Hillel of any thing which amounted to uncleanness in the eyes of the husband.
5:32:
32. πορνείας must be taken to mean sin, not only before marriage, but after it also, in a wider sense, as including μοιχεία likewise. In the similar places, Mark x. 11; Luke xvi. 18, this exception does not occur.

How far the marriage of the innocent party after separation (on account of πορνεία) is forbidden by this or the similar passage ch. xix. 9, is a weighty and difficult question. By the Roman Church such marriage is strictly forbidden, and the authority of Augustine much cited — though even he wrote late in life: 'Scripsi duos libros de conjugiis adulterinis... cupiens solvere difficillimam quæstionem. Quod utrum enodatissime fecerim nescio.' On the other hand, the Protestant and Greek Churches allow such marriage. We may well leave a matter in doubt, of which Augustine could write: 'In ipsis divinis sententiis ita obscurum est utrum et iste, cui quidem sine dubio adulteram licet dimittere, adulter tamen habeatur si alteram duxerit, ut, quantum existimo, venialiter ibi quisque fallatur.' Meyer and Stier both hold that ἀπολελυμένην can only refer to the woman unlawfully divorced, in which case there is no prohibition of the second marriage of one divorced on account of adultery.
5:33:
vv. 33–37. Fourth example. The law of oaths. 33, 34. The exact meaning of these verses is to be ascertained by two considerations. (1) That the Jews held all those oaths not to be binding, in which the sacred name of God did not directly occur, as Philo states. It therefore appears that we must understand as belonging to the quotation, 'but whatever thou shalt swear not to the Lord may be transgressed.' (2) Then our Lord passes so far beyond this rule, that He lays down the rule of the Christian community, which is not to swear at all; for that every such means of strengthening a man's simple affirmation arises out of the evil in human nature, is rendered requisite by the distrust that sin has induced, and is, therefore, out of the question among the just and true and pure of heart.

In the words 'Swear not at all,' our Lord does not so much make a positive enactment by which all swearing is to individuals forbidden (for that would be a mere technical Pharisaism wholly at variance with the spirit of the Gospel, and inconsistent with the example of God himself, Heb. vi. 13–17; vii. 21, and of the Lord when on earth, whose ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν was a solemn asseveration) as declare to us, that the proper state of Christians is, to require no oaths; that when τὸ πονηρόν is expelled from among them, every ναί and οὔ will be as decisive as an oath.
5:34: 34, 35. Compare ch. xxiii. 16–22. Archbishop Trench observes: 'Men had learned to think that, if only God's name were avoided, there was no irreverence in the frequent oaths by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem, by their own heads, and these brought in on the slightest need, or on no need at all; just as now-a-days the same lingering half-respect for the Holy Name will often cause men, who would not be wholly profane, to substitute for that name sounds that nearly resemble, but are not exactly it.' Observe that the predicates, θρόνος, ὑποπόδιον, πόλις, being placed for emphasis before the copula, are without articles.
5:36: 36. οὐ δύνασαι μίαν τρ. λ. π. ἢ μ.] Thou hast no control over the appearance of grey hairs on thy head — thy head is not thine own; thou swearest then by a creature of God, whose destinies and changes are in God's hand; so that every oath is an appeal to God.
5:37: 37. ναὶ ναὶ οὐ οὔ] The similar place in James admirably illustrates this — ἤτω ὑμῶν τὸ ναὶ ναὶ καὶ τὸ οὒ οὔ — let these words only be used, and they in simplicity and unreservedness.
5:38:
vv. 38–41. Fifth example. The law of retaliation. 38. That is, such was the public enactment of the Mosaic law, and, as such, it implied a private spirit of retaliation which should seek such redress. Here again our Lord appears to speak of the true status and perfection of a Christian community, not to forbid the infliction of judicial penalties for crime. In fact Scripture speaks, Rom. xiii. 4, of the minister of such infliction as the minister of God.

Against the notion that this sanctioned all kinds of private revenge, Augustine remarks: 'Quandoquidem et illud antiquum ad reprimendas flammas odiorum, sævientiumque immoderatos animos refrænandos, ita præceptum est... Proinde, Oculum pro oculo, dentem pro dente, non fomes sed limes furoris est; non ut id quod sopitum erat inde accenderetur, sed ne id quod ardebat ultra extenderetur impositus.'
5:39: 39. μὴ ἀντιστῆναι] Here again, we have our divine Lawgiver legislating, not in the bondage of the letter so as to stultify His disciples, but in the freedom of the spirit, laying down those great principles which ought to regulate the inner purposes and consequent actions of His followers. Taken slavishly and literally, neither did our Lord Himself conform to this precept (John xviii. 22, 23), nor his Apostles (Acts xxiii. 3). But truly, and in the spirit, our blessed Redeemer obeyed it; 'He gave his back to the smiters... and hid not his face from shame and spitting' (Isa. l. 6): and his Apostles also, see 1 Cor. iv. 9–13.
5:40:
40, 41. See note on ver. 39. κριθῆναι imports legal contention only, and is thus distinguished from the violence in ver. 39. λαβεῖν, i.e. in pledge for a debt. χιτών, the inner and less costly garment; ἱμάτιον, the outer and more valuable, used also by the poor as a coverlet by night.

ἀγγαρεύσει] Herodotus, after describing the Persian post-couriers, adds, τοῦτο τὸ δράμημα τῶν ἵππων καλέουσι Πέρσαι ἀγγαρήϊον. The Jews particularly objected to the duty of furnishing posts for the Roman government; and Demetrius, wishing to conciliate the Jews, promised, among other things, κελεύω δὲ μηδὲ ἀγγαρεύεσθαι τὰ Ἰουδαίων ὑποζύγια (Josephus).
5:42: 42. The proper understanding of the command in this verse may be arrived at from considering the way in which the Lord Himself, who declares, 'If ye shall ask any thing in my name, I will do it' (John xiv. 14), performs this promise to us. Our gracious Saviour, knowing what is good for us, so answers our prayers, that we never are sent empty away; not always, indeed, receiving what we ask, but that which in the very disappointment we are constrained thankfully to confess is better than our wish. So, in his humble sphere, should the Christian giver act. To give every thing to every one would be to act as the enemy of others and ourselves. As Chrysostom observes, μὴ τοίνυν ἁπλῶς τὰ πράγματα ἐξετάσωμεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ καιρὸν καὶ αἰτίαν καὶ γνώμην καὶ προσώπων διαφοράν.
5:43: vv. 43–48. Sixth example. The law of love and hatred. 43. The Jews called all Gentiles indiscriminately 'enemies.' In the Pharisaic interpretation therefore of the maxim (the latter part of which, although a gloss of the Rabbis, is a true representation of the spirit of the law, which was enacted for the Jews as a theocratic people), it would include the 'odium humani generis' with which the Jews were so often charged. But our Lord's fulfilment of neighbourly love extends it to all mankind — not only foreign nations, but even those who are actively employed in cursing, reviling, and persecuting us; and the hating of enemies is, in His fulfilment of it, no longer an individual or national aversion, but a coming out and being separate from all that rebel against God.
5:45:
45. ὅπως γένησθε] Probably the signification 'that ye may become' is not to be altogether lost sight of here. υἱοὶ τοῦ π., i.e. in being like Him. Τὸ μιμηταὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ, Eph. v. 1. Chrysostom beautifully observes: καίτοιγε οὐδαμοῦ τὸ γενόμενον ἴσον... σὺ μὲν γὰρ παρὰ τοῦ ὁμοδούλου καταφρονῇ, ἐκεῖνος δὲ παρὰ τοῦ δούλου καὶ μυρία εὐεργετηθέντος· καὶ σὺ μὲν ῥήματα χαρίζῃ εὐχόμενος ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ, αὐτὸς δὲ πράγματα πολὺ μεγάλα καὶ θαυμαστά, τὸν ἥλιον ἀνάπτων καὶ τοὺς ἐτησίους ὄμβρους διδούς.

Meyer quotes a sentiment of Seneca remarkably parallel: 'Si deos imitaris, da et ingratis beneficia: nam et sceleratis sol oritur, et piratis patent maria.'
5:46: 46. τελῶναι] This race of men, so frequently mentioned as the objects of hatred and contempt among the Jews, were not properly the publicans, who were wealthy Romans, of the rank of knights, farming the revenues of the provinces; but their underlings, heathens or renegade Jews, who usually exacted with recklessness and cruelty. 'The Talmud classes them with thieves and assassins, and regards their repentance as impossible' (Wordsworth).
5:47: 47. ἀσπάσησθε] Here, most probably in its literal sense. Jews did not salute Gentiles: Mohammedans do not salute Christians even now in the East.
5:48:
48. ἔσεσθε] Not altogether imperative in meaning, but including the imperative sense: such shall be the state, the aim of Christians.

τέλειοι] complete, in your love of others; not one-sided, or exclusive, as these just mentioned, but all-embracing, and God-like = οἰκτίρμονες, Luke vi. 36. No countenance is given by this verse to the ancient Pelagian or the modern heresy of perfectibility in this life. Such a sense of the words would be utterly at variance with the whole of the discourse. See especially vv. 22, 29, 32, in which the imperfections and conflicts of the Christian are fully recognized. But how far from having attained this likeness we are, St. Paul shews us (Phil. iii. 12); and every Christian feels, just in the proportion in which he has striven after it. οἱ μὲν ἀγαπῶντες τοὺς ἀγαπῶντας αὐτοὺς ἀτελεῖς εἰσιν εἰς ἀγάπην, οἱ δὲ τοὺς ἐχθρούς, τέλειοι (Euthymius).
6:1:
vv. 1–18. The Third Division of the Sermon: Warnings against Hypocritical Display, in Almsgiving, Prayer, and Fasting. 1. The discourse now moves from actions to inward motives.

δικαιοσύνην — not 'almsgiving' (a later, mistaken scribal gloss in some manuscripts, never the N.T. sense) but 'righteousness' generally, as in ch. v. 20 — the general term covering all three duties treated below.

πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι defines exactly what is condemned: not the open good deed that lets one's light shine so that men glorify God (cf. ch. v. 16), but the deed whose very aim is human praise. As Chrysostom notes, a man can act before others without doing it for display, or avoid others' sight and still secretly intend display — the inward aim is what matters.
6:2:
vv. 2–4. First example — Almsgiving. 2. μὴ σαλπίσῃς — a proverbial figure of self-advertisement, not (despite some later commentators) describing an actual literal trumpet-blowing custom among almsgivers; Lightfoot searched the Jewish sources and found 'not the least trace of a trumpet' used in giving alms.

ἀπέχουσιν — 'have in full, exhaust [their reward]' — not merely 'have their due,' but have spent the whole of what they will ever get, namely human applause.
6:3:
3, 4. μὴ γνώτω ἡ ἀριστερά σου — another popular proverbial saying, not to be pressed into a literalistic rule about the act of almsgiving itself (against De Wette), nor symbolically over-read (as even Augustine does at points); Chrysostom's plain sense is best: if it were possible to be unaware of your own good deed, that very obliviousness — simplicity of intention — is the goal.

ὁ βλέπων ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ — 'seeth in secret,' i.e. in the dark, in that hidden sphere — not 'seeth the things done in secret.'
6:5: vv. 5–15. Second example — Prayer. 5. φιλοῦσιν — 'they take delight in,' not merely 'are accustomed to.' ἑστῶτες — no special stress should be laid on the *standing* posture itself as ostentatious; it was simply the ordinary posture for prayer (cf. 1 Sam. i. 26) — as Theophylact says, 'it is not the place that harms, but the manner and the aim.'
6:6: 6. Both Chrysostom and Augustine caution against a merely literal reading: prayer in the assembly is certainly not forbidden — even a private inner room can be turned into an act of display if entered 'in order to be seen,' and conversely the true 'shutting of the door' that matters most is the shutting of the doors of the mind.
6:7:
7. βατταλογήσητε — likely an onomatopoeic word imitating stammering repetition (cf. the Battus legends in Herodotus), generally taken as 'do not make meaningless, mechanical repetitions,' though many of the Fathers extend it to praying for vain or unworthy things generally. What is forbidden is not much praying — our Lord Himself spent whole nights in prayer, and repeated the very same words at Gethsemane in His agony — but treating mere length or number of repetitions as itself a guarantee of being heard (Augustine: 'let there be no excess of words in prayer, but let urgent supplication not be absent, if fervent attention continues').

ἐθνικοί — pagans, with their pagan assumption (cf. Horace, Terence) that the gods must be wearied into hearing by sheer volume of words.
6:8: 8. Chrysostom: 'if He already knows what we need, why pray at all? Not to instruct Him, but to move Him; to grow familiar through constant approach; to be humbled; to be reminded of our own sins.'
6:9:
vv. 9–13. The Lord's Prayer. 9. Alford finds little solid evidence for the common claim that this prayer is largely drawn from pre-existing Jewish liturgical formulas — Lightfoot's parallels from the Rabbis are only the most general commonplaces.

The prayer is given, per Luke xi. 2 ('when ye pray, say...'), as both a specimen and an actual pattern of Christian prayer, not the sole permitted form (Euthymius: 'He hands down a pattern of prayer, not that we should pray only this prayer, but that, having it as a spring of prayer, we might draw from it the substance of our petitions').

Πάτερ ἡμῶν — a mode of address almost unknown to the Old Covenant in its full sense (only hinted at, e.g. Isa. lxiii. 16), impossible in its fullness until the adoption of sons had actually come through Christ. Augustine: 'This is a brotherly prayer: He does not say My Father, praying as it were only for himself, but Our Father, embracing in one prayer all who know themselves brothers in Christ.'
6:10:
10. ἐλθέτω ἡ βασιλεία σου — Augustine: 'we pray that it may come in us; we pray that we may be found in it.' Alford notes against Meyer that even the strictly Messianic-kingdom sense Meyer insists on already implicitly includes the various 'ecclesiastical and spiritual' senses some would separate from it.

γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου — not 'may our will be absorbed into thine' but 'may it be conformed and made subordinate to thine'; ὡς ἐν οὐρανῷ καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς most naturally qualifies all three preceding petitions together.
6:11: 11. ἐπιούσιον — a famously difficult word, occurring nowhere else in Greek literature, apparently coined by the Evangelists themselves (so already Origen). Alford surveys the major derivations at length (from epi + einai, 'for our subsistence,' favored by most Greek Fathers and by Tholuck; vs. epi + ienai, 'for the coming day,' favored by the Gospel of the Hebrews' 'mahar/crastinus') and concludes for the former, partly because the latter creates an apparent contradiction with ver. 34's prohibition of anxiety about tomorrow. He affirms that the petition's primary reference is to ordinary daily physical bread, while allowing — provided this physical sense stays in the foreground — a secondary, implied spiritual application to the 'Bread of Life,' since the 'us' for whom we pray is body, soul, and spirit together, all needing daily nourishment.
6:12:
12. τὰ ὀφειλήματα — sins, shortcomings (= 'trespasses,' ver. 14), specifically the ongoing post-baptismal sins of daily life, not those already remitted in baptism (Augustine).

ὡς καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀφήκαμεν — not 'in the same measure as' but 'just as, in kind' — similarity of *kind*, not degree, of forgiving act; Augustine turns this clause specifically against Pelagian claims of sinless perfection. ἀφήκαμεν (past tense) implies the act of forgiving others is to be already completed before we approach in prayer (cf. ch. v. 23, 24).
6:13:
13. 'Lead us not into temptation' must be taken in its plain, literal sense as a providential request, not (as some patristic and later writers strain to read it) merely 'do not let us be overcome once tempted' — and is not inconsistent with James i. 2's call to count trials joy, since James speaks of the inner *solicitation* to sin, not the providential permission of trial itself.

Alford rejects the closing doxology ('for thine is the kingdom...') as a later liturgical addition: it is absent from the oldest manuscripts and versions across every textual family, and from every Greek patristic commentary that expounds the prayer phrase by phrase — its eventual insertion is fully explained by the natural liturgical habit of ending prayers with an ascription of praise, whereas its supposed *omission*, had it been original, would be inexplicable.
6:14: 14, 15. Our Lord returns to expand the one clause of the prayer that needed it most, sealing it with a solemn warning (cf. Mark xi. 25; Sir. xxviii. 2, 'forgive your neighbor the wrong done to you, and then, when you pray, your sins shall be loosed').
6:16: vv. 16–18. Third example — Fasting. 16. ἀφανίζουσιν — Alford, following Tholuck, judges the best sense to be 'they disfigure' (their faces, through neglect — unwashed, unkempt) rather than simply 'covering' the face, since the contrast that follows is precisely with washing and anointing (ver. 17), not with uncovering. These verses, while not legislating the precise manner of Christian fasting, clearly assume it as a genuine and expected spiritual discipline, ranked alongside almsgiving and prayer, and subject to exactly the same demand for inward reality over outward display.
6:17: 17, 18. 'Appear as usual' — present the same face to others as if you were not fasting at all. The principle applies equally to private, voluntary fasts and to fasts more publicly enjoined, both being equally liable to ostentation.
6:19:
vv. 19–34. From hypocrisy to wholehearted dedication of the heart to God: (1) vv. 19–24, regarding earthly treasure, since one cannot serve both God and Mammon; (2) vv. 25–34, regarding earthly anxiety, on the assurance that the Father cares for us. 19, 20. The qualifying phrases ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς / ἐν οὐρανῷ belong grammatically to the verb 'treasure up,' not to the noun 'treasures.'

βρῶσις — broader than mere rust: the general 'wear and tear' of time that consumes even the finest earthly possessions (cf. Luke xii. 33; 1 Tim. vi. 19).
6:21: 21. The connexion with the preceding is plain: 'the heart is where the treasure is.' Against the objection 'why not have a treasure in both places, a divided affection?' — this very impossibility is what the following parable from nature (the eye and the body) goes on to demonstrate.
6:22:
22, 23. ὁ λύχνος — the eye as that which *lights and guides* the body, not as itself containing light, just as conscience lights the soul's faculties, but by a light not originating in itself.

ἁπλοῦς — clear, presenting a single well-defined image; πονηρός — perverse, distorting the image. φωτεινός / σκοτεινός — fully lit, as in bright sunlight, vs. fully dark, as in deep shadow — a comparison also found in Aristotle and Philo.
6:23: 23. εἰ οὖν τὸ φῶς τὸ ἐν σοὶ σκότος ἐστίν, τὸ σκότος πόσον — Alford prefers the patristic reading (Jerome, Chrysostom, Euthymius, Augustine) over the common modern flattening of this into a mere intensifier: if the conscience itself — the soul's own inner light — is darkened, how much grosser still must be the darkness of the passions and faculties that are *naturally* dark in the first place ('when the pilot is himself drowning, and the lamp itself is put out, and the leader himself taken captive, what hope remains for those under him?' — Chrysostom). The opposition is strictly between τὸ φῶς and τὸ σκότος, not a mere rhetorical exclamation about 'how great' an already-acknowledged darkness is.
6:24:
vv. 24–34. Earthly Care, and Trust in the Father. 24. δουλεύειν — not mere 'serving' but the full sense of belonging entirely to, and obeying, a master as his slave (Chrysostom: 'Job was rich, but did not serve Mammon — he possessed and ruled it; he was master, not slave'). The two suppositions (ἡ γὰρ τὸν ἕνα μισήσει... ἢ ἑνὸς ἀνθέξεται...) are not a mere repetition but mirror-image alternatives, each keeping its own reference distinct (Meyer).

μαμωνᾷ — Chaldee/Aramaic for 'riches' (from a root meaning 'to trust in'); Alford rejects the claim (Schleusner) that Mammon was the name of a Syrian deity, tracing it to a single late and unreliable source.
6:25: 25. μὴ μεριμνᾶτε — μεριμνάω (root μερίζω, 'to divide') properly means 'to be pulled in two directions, distracted'; the E.V. 'take no thought' badly overstates and so trivializes the command — 'be not anxious' is far closer to the sense.
6:26: 26. The two illustrations (birds, lilies) are not strictly parallel: the birds argue from the lesser to the greater (if God feeds them, much more will He feed us, His sons, of greater worth); the lilies add a further point — a reproof of anxiety about clothing specifically, since such glory as theirs is freely given to creatures of a far lower rank, yet is not even sought after by us in that form because it is, properly, beneath us. Note our Lord does not say 'do not sow, do not reap' — the birds are not a model for our *habits* of work, since God has made us to differ from them — but 'do not be anxious.'
6:27: 27. ἡλικίαν... πῆχυν — not stature (to which adding 'a cubit,' a foot and a half, would be an enormous addition, not the trivial one implied here and made explicit in the Lucan parallel) but length of life — life's measures rest with God alone, not with any man's own determination; the application of spatial measure-words to time is a common idiom in both Greek and Hebrew usage.
6:28: 28. καταμάθετε implies more sustained attention than the prior ἐμβλέψατε ('glance at') — birds fly past and can only be looked at; flowers remain and can be watched as they grow. Various identifications of 'the lilies of the field' have been proposed (the crown imperial fritillary, the amaryllis lutea, the Huleh lily reported by Dr. Thomson growing wild around Tabor and Nazareth itself); Alford suspects the word is meant more generally, for wildflowers as such.
6:29: 29. A declaration, from the Creator Himself, of the relative glory of all human pomp (even Solomon's, 2 Chron. ix.) set against the least of His own works — and a hint of the deeper truth that, as the flower's beauty unfolds from within by the Creator's own working, so all true human adornment must likewise be unfolded from within, not applied from without (cf. 1 Pet. iii. 3, 4).
6:30: 30. τὸν χόρτον... εἰς κλίβανον — the wild flowers of the meadow, counted together with the grass, were cut and dried for fuel in ovens in the East — a homely, vivid image of transience.
6:32: 31, 32. τὰ ἔθνη ἐπιζητοῦσιν — the Gentiles, who do not know themselves as children of a caring Father, are driven by anxious pursuit of these things; the second γάρ adds a further, independent reason beyond the birds-and-lilies argument.
6:33:
33. ζητεῖτε πρῶτον — not a temporal sequence (seek these material things only *after* finishing one's religious duties) but a statement of priority of object: let the kingdom be your great, governing concern.

τὴν δικαιοσύνην αὐτοῦ — not the forensic righteousness of justification but the spiritual purity inculcated throughout this discourse, corresponding to the τελειότης ('perfection') of ch. v. 48; in the unfolding of later Christian doctrine the righteousness of justification is indeed a necessary condition of this likeness to God, but it is not what is specifically meant in this verse.
6:34: 34. ἡ γὰρ αὔριον μεριμνήσει ἑαυτῆς — 'tomorrow will care for itself,' i.e. will bring its own full, sufficient share of cares when it comes; do not borrow tomorrow's burden and add it to today's. The closing κακία — 'sufficient for the day is its own trouble' — is itself a quiet hint that, in our present state of sin and weakness, the ideal of ver. 31 will never be perfectly realized in this life.
7:1: vv. 1–12. Of Our Conduct toward Other Men, illustrated parenthetically (vv. 7–11) by God's own benignity and wisdom toward us. The connexion with the previous chapter runs through the word κακία (vi. 34), a glance at the misery and sinfulness of human life even at its best — now followed by precepts for living rightly among others equally sinful.
7:3:
3, 4. A Rabbinic parallel exists (Rabbi Tarphon: 'I wonder whether there is anyone in this generation who will accept correction; for if one says to another, Cast out the mote from your eye, the other will answer, Cast out the beam from your own'), but used only of personal retaliation in rebuke; our Lord extends it further, to the simple incapacity of a person mired in his own sin to judge another rightly, and to the true relative scale our own faults should hold compared to our neighbor's in our own estimation — what looks like a mere mote to the onlooker is, to the person himself, a beam.

βλέπεις ('beholdest,' an outward, almost casual glance) is set against οὐ κατανοεῖς ('apprehendest not,' an inward thing already present and demanding far more attention).
7:5: 5. Euthymius: 'he calls such a man a hypocrite, as one who usurps the physician's role while himself occupying the patient's place; or as one who, under pretense of correction, busies himself with another's fault while actually aiming at condemnation.' διαβλέψεις — 'thou shalt see clearly,' with purified vision; the whole point of the saying turns on the contrast between idly *staring* at a brother's fault (βλέπειν) and actually *removing* it (ἐκβαλεῖν) — true Christian friendship's most difficult office, aimed at winning the brother (cf. ch. xviii. 15), not merely gazing at his failure.
7:6: 6. τὸ ἅγιον — most likely alludes to the sacrificial meat offered in the Temple, which no unclean person might eat (Lev. xxii. 6 ff.) — the same term later used by the early Church for the consecrated Eucharistic elements. As Archbishop Trench notes, the point is not that dogs would refuse the holy food (they would relish it) but that to give it to them at all is itself the profanation. The connexion with the surrounding verses: 'judge not... attempt not to correct others when you need correction far more yourself... yet do not be so naive as to fail to discern character — give not what is holy to dogs.'
7:7: vv. 7–11. A parenthetical assurance of God's generosity, answering the implicit objection: 'if discernment in giving is the standard even for us, what then can I expect from God?' 7. The three verbs (ask, seek, knock) form a deliberate climax — Chrysostom: 'from knocking, [our Lord moves us] to approach with vehemence and a fervent mind in our prayer.'
7:8: 8. The only qualification to this repeated promise is supplied by vv. 9–11 below, and by James iv. 3 ('ye ask and receive not, because ye ask amiss').
7:9: 9, 10. A broken construction (anacoluthon) after the first question, as also at ch. xii. 11; Luke's parallel adds the egg and the scorpion to the fish and the serpent.
7:11: 11. πονηροί — evil only by comparison with God; not a rebuke but a general statement of human corruption and weakness, addressed, as Augustine notes, to the very same disciples just taught to say 'Our Father.' Stier calls this verse 'the strongest dictum probans for original sin in the whole of Holy Scripture.' ἀγαθά — principally the Holy Spirit Himself, per the parallel in Luke xi. 13.
7:12:
12. Augustine answers the charge (echoed later by Gibbon) that the Golden Rule was already stated by pagan philosophers like Pythagoras and Plato: 'If any of them is found to have said what Christ also said, we congratulate him, but we do not follow him... O man, attend to Christ, not as to when He came to you, but as to when He made you.'

οὕτως refers back to ὅσα ἂν θέλητε, not to ταῦτα — a crucial distinction: we are not to do to others simply whatever *we* happen to want, but to ask what *they* would reasonably want done to them, and act on that.
7:13: vv. 13–27. The Conclusion of the Discourse: the dangers of hypocrisy, in being led astray by false teachers and in one's own inner life. 13. The image of a gate standing at the end of a road has a striking classical parallel in the Tablet of Cebes: 'do you see a small gate, and a road before it not much traveled, where very few go? — that is the road leading to true education.'
7:14: 14. ὅτι gives a second, deeper reason underlying ver. 13: the way to destruction is broad precisely *because* so few find the narrow way of life — not because God has arbitrarily ordained the loss of the many (He wills all to come to the knowledge of the truth), but because so few actually come to Christ for life, the rest perishing in their own sin (cf. ch. xxv. 41). Alford rejects the alternative reading 'how narrow is the gate!' as both grammatically forced and inconsistent with the following ὀλίγοι εἰσίν.
7:15: vv. 15–20. Warning against false prophets. 15. These ψευδοπροφῆται point directly forward to the false prophets of ch. xxiv. 24, and indirectly to such deceivers in every age; ἐνδύμασιν προβάτων probably means simply that they adopt the outward manner and appearance of the sheep themselves to gain entry, rather than any specific reference to prophetic dress.
7:16: 16. καρποί here means both their corrupt doctrine and their vicious practice, as opposed to the mere outward show — almsgiving, prayer, fasting — that is their 'sheep's clothing.' Augustine: 'we look for the fruits of love, and find the thorns of dissension.'
7:17: 17, 18. Alford notes that the Manichæans wrongly cited these verses to defend their doctrine of two opposed natures (good and evil); Augustine answers that this reading contradicts the entire scope of the passage (cf. ver. 13) — 'a bad tree cannot bear good fruit, but it can be made good, so that it bears good fruit.' Conversely, these same verses served Augustine against the shallow Pelagian notion that human deeds can be judged in isolation from the inner root from which they grow.
7:20: 20. ἐπιγνώσεσθε — stronger than mere γνώσεσθε: 'ye shall *thoroughly* know them' (cf. 1 Cor. xiii. 12).
7:21:
vv. 21–23. The doom of hypocrites, leading into the closing parable. 21. Notice that our Lord here sets Himself forth as Judge on the great day, and speaks not of 'my will' but 'the will of my Father' — an important doctrinal landmark this early in His ministry as recorded by Matthew.

οὐ πᾶς ≠ 'no one' (against Elsner, Fritzsche) — the wording requires a partitive sense, 'not everyone,' referring here to mere lip-confession, distinct from the deeper, genuine confession of 1 Cor. xii. 3.
7:22: 22. ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ — the prophetic 'day of the Lord,' as the Jews themselves spoke of the day of judgment simply as 'that day.' ἐπροφητεύσαμεν — 'preached,' not necessarily 'foretold the future' (cf. 1 Cor. xii. 10).
7:23: 23. ὅτι here is recitative ('I will declare to them plainly...'), not causal as some have proposed — an arrangement without precedent in this construction. ὁμολογήσω is a striking word here: a statement of the plain, simple truth, set against the false self-coloring of the hypocrites — 'I will tell them the plain truth.' οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς — 'know' in the sense of John x. 14 ('I know my sheep, and am known of mine'): neither preaching in Christ's name nor performing miracles in it is an infallible mark of genuine discipleship — only a life truly devoted to the Father's will, which that knowledge produces.
7:24: vv. 24–27. The Two Builders. 24. πᾶς οὖν ὅστις is a pendent nominative, a construction with classical parallels (e.g. in Plato); note the deliberate use of ὅστις rather than the simple ὅς throughout — ὅς merely identifies, ὅστις classifies, generalizing the description into a type.
7:25: 25. This parable should not be pressed into an allegory of detail (rain, floods, wind as three distinct kinds of trial); but the Rock as a figure for the speaker Himself is far too frequent and deliberate a biblical image (2 Sam. xxii. 2, 32; Ps. xviii. 2; xxviii. 1; Isa. xxvi. 4; 1 Cor. x. 4, etc.) to be overlooked here. To build on the rock is to hear Christ's words and bring one's whole life into conformity with His expressed will, thereby standing, by faith, in living union with Him.
7:27: 27. μεγάλη — the fall is 'all the greater' precisely because this is a *professed* disciple — one who has heard the words — and therefore has further to fall in apostasy than one who never heard them at all.
7:28: vv. 28, 29. Conclusion. ἦν διδάσκων — the periphrastic imperfect spreads the description over the whole course of His teaching, not merely this one sermon. Chrysostom: 'He did not, like the prophets or Moses, refer His sayings to another, but everywhere showed Himself to be the one holding authority — continually adding, when laying down the law, But I say unto you — and, reminding them of that [judgment] day, showed Himself to be the very Judge.'
8:1: vv. 1–4. Healing of a Leper. Mark i. 40–45; Luke v. 12–14. With this and the following chapter begins a solemn procession of miracles confirming the authority with which our Lord had just spoken — Euthymius: 'He passes from teaching to wonders; lest, having taught as one having authority, He should be thought to boast or exaggerate, He now shows His authority in deeds also, and confirms His words from His works.'
8:2:
2. Leprosy was specifically chosen under the Mosaic law, Alford argues at length (citing Trench), not for sanitary reasons but as the most loathsome and incurable disease available to represent the defilement of sin on the once-pure human body — 'a living death,' using the same rites of exclusion and cleansing as those for contact with the dead (cf. Num. xix; Lev. xiv). The Jews, from Isa. liii. 4, even held a tradition that the Messiah himself would be a leper.

κύριε — not a mere title of courtesy but an expression of faith in Jesus as Messiah (Stier: 'this is the right utterance of Kyrie, which will never be made in vain').
8:3: 3. ἥψατο αὐτοῦ — having just fulfilled the law in word, He now fulfills it in deed: the law itself forbade touching a leper (Lev. v. 3), exactly as it forbade healing on the Sabbath, both ceremonial restrictions superseded by the same almighty power that suspends natural law altogether. Alford suggests the touch is also symbolic of Christ's taking on Himself, laying hold of, our (fallen) human nature (cf. Heb. ii. 16).
8:4: 4. Alford weighs three explanations of the command to silence: (1) a moral admonition against boastfulness, of lasting force; (2) a merely temporary, cautionary measure to avoid the priests obstructing his certification out of malice; (3), which Alford judges correct, our Lord's near-uniform pattern of suppressing the fame of His miracles, so that He might be known as Messiah by the ultimate fruit of His work rather than by wonder-working power alone (cf. ch. xii. 15–21, citing Isa. xlii). On 'show thyself to the priest,' Alford notes this verse has been pressed (wrongly, he argues, quoting Gratian and Peter Lombard against their own conclusions) into support of a sacramental theory of priestly absolution; properly understood it shows precisely the opposite — Christ alone cleanses, the priestly judgment being only a public, after-the-fact recognition.
8:5: vv. 5–13. Healing of the Centurion's Servant. Luke vii. 1–10 gives a fuller account of the opening of this episode (the centurion sending elders rather than coming himself) — an example, Alford notes via Augustine's reply to the Manichæan Faustus, of the common and unremarkable variation between a condensed account (a man 'doing' something) and a fuller one (the same man doing it 'through another'), which should not be read as contradiction.
8:6: 6. παῖς — Luke clarifies this was a δοῦλος 'who was dear to him'; Calvin notes this detail forestalls the reader's natural doubt, since slaves were not ordinarily objects of such anxious concern unless, as evidently here, of unusual character and fidelity.
8:8: 8. The centurion, on hearing the Lord was actually coming (Luke vii. 6), sent a second, still humbler message: as a Gentile he felt himself outside the commonwealth of Israel, unworthy to receive Israel's Redeemer under his own roof.
8:9: 9. The centurion's logic: 'I know how to obey, being myself under authority, and how to be obeyed, having soldiers under me — how much more, then, art Thou obeyed, Lord over all, whom even diseases serve as their Master!' This military, practical cast of mind, rather than weakening, is what our Lord singles out for special commendation.
8:10: 10, 11. Augustine, citing this passage at length: 'how widely has the wild olive spread! This world was a bitter forest: but because of his humility, because of "I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof," many shall come from the East and the West... And what of those who were of Abraham's own stock? What befalls the ruins with which the tree was full? Only that they shall be cut off, that these others may be grafted in.' ἐθαύμασεν — to be accepted simply as historical fact, like our Lord's weeping or rejoicing elsewhere, not explained away as merely 'a lesson in what to admire'; the genuine mysteries of His true humanity are too precious to be sacrificed to theological timidity.
8:12: 12. οἱ υἱοὶ τῆς βασιλείας — the natural heirs, disinherited through their own rebellion. τὸ σκότος τὸ ἐξώτερον — the darkness *outside* the lit banquet hall (cf. ch. xxii. 13). These verses are absent from Luke's version of this episode and recur, on a quite different occasion, at ch. xiii. 28, 29.
8:13: 13. The precise nature of the servant's illness is unclear — Luke says he 'was about to die'; Matthew, that he was 'grievously tormented' — but Alford notes a close parallel disease description in 1 Macc. ix. 55, 56, suggesting perhaps an attack of tetanus (anciently classed under 'paralysis'), more common in hot climates, rather than apoplexy (which typically removes sensation rather than causing torment).
8:14: vv. 14–17. Healing of Peter's Mother-in-law, and Many Others. Mark i. 29–34; Luke iv. 38–41 (both fuller here than Matthew). The phrase common to all three — 'the fever left her' — together with her immediately rising to serve, shows the fever did not merely subside naturally (which would have left her weak and exhausted) but was instantly, completely reversed.
8:16: 16. The sick were brought at evening — possibly for the relative coolness, possibly because the day's labor (and so the availability of bearers) was over, or, very plausibly, because it was the Sabbath, which ended at sunset (cf. Mark i. 21, 29, 32).
8:17: 17. This citation of Isa. liii. 4 differs from the LXX. Alford rejects the merely weak readings of ἔλαβεν/ἐβάστασεν as simply 'took away'/'healed' (which empties αὐτός of its emphatic force) and the view that it refers to Christ's own personal fatigue from prolonged healing; he holds instead that the true relevance of the prophecy lies in seeing these miracles as lesser, typical previews of the great work of bearing the sin of the world that Christ came to accomplish — diseases themselves being, throughout Scripture, testimonies to and types of the effect of sin, and Christ's compassion in healing them being a genuine, costly 'suffering with' (the literal sense of compassion) rather than a merely external display of power.
8:18: vv. 18–ix. 1. Jesus Crosses the Lake; Incidents before Embarking; the Stilling of the Storm; the Gadarene Demoniacs. Mark iv. 35–v. 20; Luke ix. 57–60; viii. 22–39.
8:19: 19. Both following incidents (vv. 19–22) are placed by Luke much later, during the final journey to Jerusalem. Alford judges it historically untenable (against harmonizers like Greswell) that two such distinctive incidents happened identically twice; he treats this kind of discrepancy not as something to be explained away at all costs but as a valuable, honest indicator for the careful student of how the Gospel traditions actually took shape.
8:20: 20. ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου — drawn from Dan. vii. 13, understood by the Jews themselves (John xii. 34; Luke xxii. 69, 70) as equivalent to 'Son of God' / Messiah. It is our Lord's own characteristic, self-chosen title — encompassing in one pregnant phrase His identity as the Son of God manifest in human flesh, the second Adam, and all the conditions of humiliation, suffering, and exaltation that title entails.
8:21: 21. Per Clement of Alexandria's tradition, this may be the same disciple (traditionally identified as Philip) whom Christ had, according to a separate strand of tradition, already called to 'follow Me' much earlier; if so, ἀκολούθει μοι here would be not a first call but an admonition occasioned by some slackness on the disciple's part (cf. John xxi. 19, 22).
8:22: 22. νεκρούς used in two different senses in the same short sentence — first spiritually ('let the [spiritually] dead bury their own [literally] dead'), exactly as our Lord similarly plays on two senses of 'life/death' in John xi. 25, 26. Euthymius: our Lord did not forbid honoring parents, but taught that one who aspires to heavenly things should not turn back to earthly ones, nor abandon the living-giving pursuit to run back to the things of death — He knew others would bury the man, and (Euthymius surmises) the deceased may not even have been a believer.
8:23: 23. This crossing is placed by Mark and Luke after the parable discourse of ch. xiii., with Mark specifying it occurred 'that same day, when evening was come' (Mark iv. 35).
8:24: 24. σεισμός — usually 'earthquake,' here a violent commotion of the sea (= Mark/Luke's λαῖλαψ, 'squall'); καλύπτεσθαι, kept in its strict imperfect force ('was becoming covered'), needs no softening — all lakes ringed by mountains, and hilly coastlines generally, are subject to such sudden violent gusts.
8:25: 25. Alford cites with approval Augustine's important methodological remark on the three differently-worded cries recorded by the Synoptists (Matthew's 'Lord, save us, we perish,' Mark's 'Master, carest thou not that we perish?', Luke's 'Master, master, we perish'): it is one and the same essential meaning expressed by those crying out and wishing to be saved, and it is futile labor to insist on settling which exact words were spoken — would that all such apparent discrepancies were treated with this same wisdom, rather than 'spending time knitting cobwebs.'
8:26: 26. They were 'of little faith' in fearing to perish while the sleeping Savior was aboard, yet not faithless, since they did turn to Him for help; hence He both grants their prayer completely (stilling the storm) and rebukes them for not having had the stronger faith to trust Him even while He seemed indifferent to their danger. Alford notes, without overpressing it, the long-recognized symbolic resonance of the scene: the Saviour and His disciples in the storm-tossed ship recall the Ark bearing humanity on the flood, and foreshadow the Church, tossed by the world's tempests yet never without Him.
8:28: vv. 28–34. The Gadarene Demoniacs. Alford gives an extended geographical discussion of the textual variants Gadarenes/Gerasenes/Gergesenes: he concludes, against Origen's preference for 'Gergesa' (a town Origen could not actually verify existed near the lake in his own day) and against 'Gerasa' (a city far too distant from any lake), that 'Gadarenes' — referring to the well-documented city of Gadara, a member of the Decapolis whose broader territory plausibly extended to the lakeshore — is both the best-attested and most geographically coherent reading.
8:29: 29. τί ἡμῖν καὶ σοί — a Hebraism (cf. 2 Sam. xvi. 10); πρὸ καιροῦ is peculiar to Matthew's account, implying the demons' awareness that a final, appointed judgment still lay ahead of this present encounter.
8:30: 30. μακράν — 'at a distance,' against the Vulgate's 'not far,' and consistent with Mark's and Luke's notice that the swine were on the hillside while the scene of the miracle itself was apparently on the plain below.
8:31: 31. Mark and Luke supply the demons' stated motive: not to be sent 'into the abyss' — i.e., out of their permitted earthly range altogether into a place of confined, pre-judgment torment.
8:32: vv. 32–34. Alford here inserts a lengthy excursus on demoniacal possession generally, to be referred back to throughout the Gospels. His main points: (1) the Gospel narratives stake their own historical truthfulness on these events being real, not mere accommodation to contemporary opinion — our Lord Himself speaks of the demons' personality and presence directly (cf. Luke xi. 17–26), and it is incompatible with His perfect truthfulness to suppose He spoke so plainly, repeatedly, in encouragement of a mere superstition He knew to be false; (2) possession is everywhere in the Gospels distinguished from ordinary bodily disease, not collapsed into it (cf. ch. ix. 32, 33); (3) the demoniac, unlike the merely wicked man given over to sin, is an object of compassion, not punishment — Scripture suggests a 'double consciousness,' the oppressed true self at times crying out for mercy even while overpowered; (4) the apparent absence of comparable cases in the modern world is unsurprising given that our Lord's earthly ministry fell at a uniquely concentrated crisis-point of spiritual conflict, when 'the hour and power of darkness' was permitted unusual scope, though Alford does not rule out that some modern cases of insanity may still have a similarly direct spiritual cause; (5) on the destruction of the swine, this is no more inherently 'unmerciful' an act than the cursing of the fig tree (ch. xxi. 18–22) — God who ordains the daily slaughter of animals for human food may equally permit their destruction for human spiritual instruction or deliverance.
9:1: vv. 1–8. Healing of a Paralytic. Mark ii. 1–12; Luke v. 17–26.
9:2: 2. ἀφέωνται — a perfect-passive form (cognate with the perfect-active ἀφέωκα), treated by ancient grammarians variously as a Doric or Attic survival; in either case, a settled state of forgiveness, not a mere future intention.
9:4: 4. ἰδών — by the spiritual power dwelling within Him (cf. John ii. 24, 25); Mark's parallel, 'perceiving in His spirit,' is more precise still — comparable to John xi. 33's 'groaned in the spirit,' i.e. 'groaning within Himself.'
9:5: 5. Trench's point, which Alford quotes approvingly, is crucial to the logic: our Lord does not ask which is intrinsically *easier*, forgiving sins or healing a paralytic (it cannot be said that forgiving is in itself easier than healing) — but which is easier to *claim*, since only one of the two claims admits of immediate, visible verification. By doing the provable thing (healing), He vindicates His authority to do the unprovable thing (forgiving) as well — by these visible tokens of God's grace, showing in which direction the deeper, invisible currents of that same grace are flowing.
9:6:
6. ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου — equivalent in Jewish understanding to 'the Christ, the Son of God' (cf. ch. xxvi. 63; John v. 27). Trench notes how the Alexandrian Fathers, against the Nestorians, drew on this very interchangeability of titles to argue for the full communication of properties between Christ's two natures in His one Person — though Alford, with Trench, prefers to read 'Son of Man' here simply as our Lord's own characteristic, chosen self-designation, sometimes pressed for its full theological weight, sometimes used more simply as equivalent to 'Messiah.'

ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς — deliberately distinguished from 'in heaven' (cf. ch. xvi. 19; xviii. 18); Bengel: 'this saying has the very savor of a heavenly origin' — the Son of Man, as God manifest in human flesh, exercises on earth that authority which belongs essentially to God in heaven, not by delegation but because, being God, He is also the Son of Man (John v. 27).
9:8: 8. τοῖς ἀνθρώποις — not 'to a man' nor 'for men's benefit' but 'to mankind' generally: the crowd's own words, even without their grasping the full weight of what they said, were true in the highest sense.
9:9:
vv. 9–17. The Calling of Matthew; the Feast; the Question about Fasting. Mark ii. 13–22; Luke v. 27–39. Alford weighs at length the long-debated question of whether 'Matthew' here is identical with 'Levi' in Mark and Luke — concluding for identity (the near-verbatim parallel narratives, the universal early consensus, and the natural explanation that Matthew, in his own Gospel, simply uses his apostolic name throughout, exactly as Mark and Luke do when *they* list him among the Twelve) despite some intriguing but ultimately inconclusive patristic traces of an older tradition distinguishing the two.

λεγόμενον — not implying any other prior name, simply 'called Matthew' (cf. ch. ii. 23).
9:10: 10. Alford rejects Greswell's attempt to separate this feast from the nearly identical one in Mark/Luke on the grounds of supposed verbal inconsistencies (e.g. the use of the article with 'house,' or with 'boat' at ch. viii. 23, which Alford shows elsewhere to be generic, not specifying any one particular house or boat); he judges Greswell's harmonizing arguments here unconvincing and the three accounts plainly the same event.
9:11: 11. These Pharisees were local to the place (Luke specifies 'their scribes'); the circumstances of the remonstrance (spoken *to* the disciples, but *heard* by our Lord) imply an occasion adjoining, but not strictly identical with, the feast itself.
9:12: 12. Both ἰσχύοντες ('whole') and κακῶς ἔχοντες ('sick') must be read subjectively — according to the Pharisees' own self-estimate, an 'ironic concession' (Calvin, Meyer) — not as Alford's own objective judgment that the Pharisees really were spiritually whole.
9:13: 13. πορευθέντες μάθετε answers to a common Talmudic formula. The citation (Hosea vi. 6) is given nearly verbatim in Mark (with ὑγιαίνοντες for ἰσχύοντες) and Luke (with ἐλήλυθα for ἦλθον, and the addition 'unto repentance').
9:14: vv. 14–17. The Question about Fasting. 14. Per Mark's fuller account, it was the disciples of John *and* of the Pharisees together who raised the question — one of several places where the three Gospels mutually confirm and complete one another, a detail mentioned only incidentally by one Evangelist becoming the leading point in another's fuller narrative. The frequent fasting of John's disciples reflects not mourning for their master's imprisonment but the general ascetic discipline John, as a preacher of repentance, inculcated.
9:15:
15. ὁ νυμφίος — a title with peculiar force addressed specifically to John's disciples, since their own master had already said of himself, 'He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom's voice — this joy of mine, therefore, is fulfilled' (John iii. 29). In calling Himself the Bridegroom, our Lord announces the fulfillment of a whole cycle of O.T. prophetic imagery (Hosea, and especially Isa. liv. 5–10) in which Israel's God is figured as Bridegroom to His people. Stier notes that here, unusually, the parable itself seems to have grown out of the emphatic title rather than the reverse.

ἐλεύσονται δὲ ἡμέραι... ὅταν ἀπαρθῇ — a strikingly calm, early foreshadowing by our Lord of His own coming death. The later fasting envisioned is not an arbitrary ecclesiastical ordinance but the genuine, spontaneous expression of real sorrow at the Bridegroom's literal absence — a principle Alford applies to Christian fasting generally: it should spring from genuine inward spiritual need, not from externally fixed and obligatory observance (he notes pointedly that in the Reformed churches the formally retained fast-days are widely neglected even by devout believers, while genuine providential occasions for fasting are kept with real solemnity).
9:16: 16, 17. The two parables (patch, wineskins) contrast the old and new dispensations on the specific point at issue (fasting), with the imagery of a wedding running through both, connecting them to the preceding verses. The new patch's very completeness and strength is what tears away from the surrounding old, weakened cloth, producing 'a worse rent' — a tear now extending *beyond* the bounds of the original tear, not merely deepening it (against the E.V.'s 'the rent is made worse'). Stier notes the sadly prophetic force of this image in later Church history's repeated attempts to patch evangelical truth onto the old ceremonial system.
9:17: See 9:16. This second parable is not a mere repetition of the first but advances further, from the outward (the garment) to the inward (the wine, the spirit of the system itself): the old, unrenewed man (the ἀσκὸς παλαιός) simply cannot contain the new wine of the Gospel — it shatters him, and both the man and the wine are equally lost (ῥήγνυνται οἱ ἀσκοί... ὁ οἶνος ἐκχεῖται).
9:18: vv. 18–26. The Raising of Jairus's Daughter, and the Healing of the Woman with an Issue of Blood. Mark v. 21–43; Luke viii. 41–56, both substantially fuller than Matthew's compressed account here. ἄρτι ἐτελεύτησεν — she was not yet dead but dying, at the very point of death; Matthew, characteristically compressing, omits the later message from the house reporting her actual death (cf. Mark v. 35; Luke viii. 49).
9:20: 20. κράσπεδον — the fringe or tassel commanded to be worn on the corners of the outer garment as a sign of consecration to God (cf. Num. xv. 38); the definite article indicates the particular tassel actually touched.
9:22: 22. Per Mark and Luke's fuller accounts, the cure occurred at the touch itself, before our Lord's words; He then asked who had touched Him, perceiving that power had gone out from Him, and the woman, aware of what had happened, came forward trembling to confess it.
9:24: 24. No inference about the reality of the child's death can be drawn from 'she is not dead, but sleeping': our Lord uses an exactly parallel expression of the already-dead Lazarus (John xi. 11), in both cases with reference to the imminent awakening soon to follow, not as a denial of actual death. Luke's addition, 'knowing that she was dead,' shows the Evangelist himself recognized no mere apparent death was meant.
9:25: 25. From the fuller parallel accounts: our Lord took with Him only Peter, James, John, and the parents; the girl was twelve years old and an only daughter (Luke viii. 42); His actual Aramaic words, preserved by Mark, were Talitha cumi.
9:27: vv. 27–31. Healing of Two Blind Men (peculiar to Matthew). 27. υἱὸς Δαυείδ — Euthymius: 'they cry this out in His honor, for this title was held in the highest regard among the Jews.' It is striking that in all three accounts of giving sight to the blind recorded in this Gospel, this same title 'Son of David' appears.
9:29: 29. A distinctive feature of this miracle: no direct word of healing power is spoken; instead our Lord makes a conditional concession ('according to your faith be it unto you'), making the result itself a direct measure of their faith. Stier notes a discernible pattern across this period of the ministry: our Lord moves from granting healing immediately on request to increasingly testing and exercising the faith of those who come to Him.
9:30: 30. ἐνεβριμήθη — to charge with severity, sternly. Alford suggests a double purpose behind our Lord's urgent insistence on silence here: (1) to avoid being so overwhelmed with requests as to have no time or strength left for preaching the Gospel itself; (2) to avoid prematurely arousing the Pharisees' hostile attention before His appointed hour. The two men's open disobedience to this solemn charge — however well-intentioned — Alford notes pointedly was itself a fault, not (as some Roman Catholic interpreters have read it) a praiseworthy zeal: obedience is better than even the most well-meant self-willed enthusiasm.
9:32: vv. 32–34. Healing of a Dumb Demoniac (peculiar to Matthew, though closely related to the similar episode at ch. xii. 22 and its parallel in Luke xi. 14 — Alford judges these probably distinct incidents, the Pharisees' Beelzebub slander being a charge they would naturally have repeated more than once, rather than one episode duplicated in the record).
9:33: 33. ἐφάνη οὕτως — 'never was it seen [to produce results] like this': οὕτως here means 'thus, in this manner,' not merely 'such a thing' as some have proposed.
9:35: vv. 35–38. Our Lord's Compassion for the Multitude (peculiar to Matthew), introducing the calling and commissioning of the Twelve exactly as ch. iv. 23–25 introduced the Sermon on the Mount — both discourses framed, deliberately, with this same indefiniteness of date. From the other Evangelists (Mark iii. 16; Luke vi. 13) it is clear the Twelve had actually been chosen and named some time before this point, and likely spent further time with our Lord before being formally sent out.
9:36: 36. ἐσκυλμένοι — harassed, worn out, whether literally by the exertion of following Him or spiritually under the crushing weight of Scribal and Pharisaic tradition (cf. ch. xxiii. 4); ἐριμμένοι — 'cast aside, neglected,' like sheep that have wandered from their proper pasture and care. The context shows His compassion was specifically stirred by their lack of true spiritual shepherds.
9:38: 37, 38. The harvest here is primarily the Jewish people themselves, whose multitude moved our Lord's compassion. Chrysostom notes the lesson of humility embedded in His sending out others rather than doing everything Himself: 'so that He might not draw everyone to Himself alone' — and also so that the disciples themselves might be trained, as if in a wrestling-school in Palestine, for the larger contests of the whole world that lay ahead of them.
10:1: ch. x. 1–xi. 1. The Mission of the Twelve Apostles. Mark vi. 7–13; Luke ix. 1–6 (for the sending out); Mark iii. 13–19; Luke vi. 13–16 (for the calling and naming, recorded earlier — this is their *mission*, not their original choosing, which had taken place some time before).
10:2:
vv. 2–4. The Twelve Apostles. Alford compares the four N.T. lists of the Twelve (here; Mark iii. 16; Luke vi. 14; Acts i. 13) in detail: all four agree on three fixed groups of four, with Peter, Philip, and James of Alphæus always heading their respective groups and Judas Iscariot always last — though the internal order within each group of four varies (Matthew and Luke's Gospel pair the disciples by their order of calling and by being sent out two-by-two; Mark and Acts group by personal prominence).

πρῶτος (of Peter) — not mere priority of listing or of calling, but primus inter pares, attested by his consistent prominence throughout the Gospels and Acts (speaking for the Twelve, addressed by our Lord as representative even among the three favored disciples, presiding at the first apostolic council). Alford is emphatic, however, that no later Roman primacy can be read out of this: no trace of such a claim appears in any other Apostle's writings, nor in Peter's own epistles, where he calls himself merely a 'fellow-elder' (1 Pet. v. 1) and addresses his readers as having received faith 'of like value' to his own (2 Pet. i. 1).
10:3: 3. Alford works through the identifications: Bartholomew (son of Talmai) is very probably Nathanael of Cana, on several converging lines of evidence from John i. 45 ff.; Thomas (Didymus) and Matthew the tax-collector are explicitly linked here with Matthew's own earlier call (ch. ix. 9); James the son of Alphæus may be identical with 'James the Less,' son of the Mary married to Clopas (if Alphæus = Clopas, as the Greek and Aramaic forms plausibly suggest) — and so possibly the same as the 'James the Lord's brother' of Gal. i. 19, though Alford notes real difficulties with this identification elsewhere. Lebbæus/Thaddæus (a genuinely unsettled textual and historical question) is generally taken as the same person as 'Judas of James' in Luke's two lists.
10:4:
4. Σίμων ὁ καναναῖος — not a place-name but a transliteration of the Hebrew/Aramaic equivalent of ζηλωτής ('Zealot,' so Luke), suggesting Simon belonged before his call to the militant nationalist sect that, following Phinehas's example (Num. xxv. 7, 8), took the law into its own hands against perceived offenders — a sect whose zealotry eventually helped bring about Jerusalem's destruction.

Ἰούδας ὁ Ἰσκαριώτης — most likely 'a man of Kerioth' in Judah, son of a Simon (John vi. 71; xiii. 2, 26); Alford notes 'Iscariot' cannot be a mere surname, as the full triple form 'Judas, son of Simon, Iscariot' shows.
10:5:
vv. 5–15. The First Part of the Mission Discourse: instructions for the immediate journey to the cities of Israel. Comparing this verse with ch. xi. 1, this discourse was delivered as one continuous address on the occasion of the Twelve's first sending; many of its themes recur later, adapted, in the sending of the Seventy (Luke x. 2 ff.). Its primary reference is to that immediate first mission, but it includes, in seed form, instruction for the Church's ministry to the end of time.

Σαμαρειτῶν — the mixed-descent, partly-idolatrous inhabitants of the region between Judæa and Galilee (cf. 2 Kings xvii. 24–41), with whom Jews had no ordinary dealings (John iv. 9); this restriction was strictly temporary and judicial — it is explicitly lifted in Acts i. 8, and the result is recorded in Acts viii.
10:7: 7. This proclamation ('the kingdom of heaven is at hand') marks the preparatory character of this first mission, in contrast with the fuller message later entrusted to the Church (cf. Col. i. 26–28).
10:9: 9, 10. All the prohibited items (no gold/silver/bronze in the belt; no scrip for the journey; no second tunic, sandals, or staff) fall under the single verb κτήσησθε ('procure'), explained by Mark's and Luke's parallel 'take nothing for the journey' — they were to set out in complete dependence on the One who sent them, making no special advance preparation. Alford notes this prohibition, like the Sabbath law's strict letter, was for that journey only, later explicitly rescinded (cf. Luke xxii. 35, 36).
10:10: 10. ἄξιος γὰρ ὁ ἐργάτης — a common-life truth (a laborer deserves his wage) elevated here to its highest sense, applied to laborers in Christ's own vineyard (cf. 1 Cor. ix. 13, 14). Stier rightly warns against the 'gross perversion' of binding modern ministers to the bare letter of this command (forbidding any provision whatsoever) while still holding that they remain bound by its underlying spirit.
10:11: 11. ἄξιος — 'inclined to receive you and your message,' worthy of being your host — comparable to those 'ordained to eternal life' in Acts xiii. 48. This brief command is expanded much more fully in Luke x. 7 ff.
10:12: 12, 13. τὴν οἰκίαν — not necessarily the worthy person's house specifically (that would already be settled by ver. 11) but any house entered, to be tested by the subsequent inquiry. ἡ εἰρήνη ὑμῶν — the customary Eastern greeting of peace, to be offered regardless of the household's worthiness; if unworthy, the blessing simply 'returns' unfulfilled, as though never spoken (Euthymius: 'let it work nothing, but take it back with you as you leave').
10:14: 14. The shaking off of dust carries one of two related meanings: either total disassociation ('we take nothing of yours, not even your dust, with us' — Luke x. 11), or specifically a refusal to share in the guilt of rejecting God's message (cf. 1 Sam. ii. 5, where shoes on the feet are figured as sharing in bloodguilt) — a gesture elsewhere used by Pharisees re-entering Judæa from Gentile lands to renounce contact with Gentile soil.
10:15: 15. The first of several 'Amen I say unto you' formulas with which our Lord marks the close of each section of this discourse. This denunciation, like the command to shake off dust, applies strictly to Israel, long prepared by the Law, Prophets, and John for this message — not, at this stage, to Gentiles who had never received any such preparation.
10:16: vv. 16–23. The Second Part of the Discourse: the wider apostolic mission, including persecution, foreshadowed beyond the immediate journey. 16. ἐγώ is emphatic, recalling who it is that sends them (Euthymius: 'I, who am able to do all things'). The image of sheep among wolves applied to Israel among the Gentiles has Rabbinic parallels noted by Stier; an early extra-canonical saying of the Lord (in Clement's second epistle) expands it memorably: when Peter asks what becomes of the lambs if the wolves tear them apart, Jesus answers, 'let the lambs not fear the wolves after they are dead, and you, do not fear those who kill you and can do nothing more — but fear Him who, after you are dead, has authority over soul and body, to cast into the fire of Gehenna.'
10:17: 17. προσέχετε turns from inward character (serpent-wisdom, dove-simplicity) to outward circumstance. συνέδρια — the local courts of seven established in every city (cf. Deut. xvi. 18; ch. v. 21), here perhaps used more generally for any court or tribunal.
10:18: 18. ἡγεμόνας — Roman provincial governors (Pilate, Felix, Festus); βασιλεῖς — client kings (Herod, Agrippa). The previous verse spoke of Jewish persecution; this, of Gentile — together comprising 'a testimony to them and to the Gentiles,' the same double-edged witness (for some, against others) that always belongs to the preached word of God (cf. Rev. i. 16, 'a two-edged sword').
