He firmly rejects Meyer's view that our Lord here predicted His own final, still-future Parousia while not knowing its timing (Mark xiii. 32) — calling this self-contradictory, since it is one thing not to know a date and quite another to issue a determinate, solemnly-introduced prophecy ('Amen I say to you...') about it. He also sharply rejects Wordsworth's allegorizing softening of 'shall not taste death' into 'shall not taste its bitterness,' which Alford judges inverts the saying's plain sense entirely.
17:1:
vv. 1–13. The Transfiguration. Mark ix. 2–13; Luke ix. 28–36. This solemn event marks our Lord's formal installation into His coming sufferings. The same three Apostles (Peter, James, John) had earlier witnessed His power over death (Mark v. 37) and would later accompany Him in Gethsemane and be especially privileged witnesses of the Resurrection. Moses and Elijah, representing the Law and the Prophets, had each left the world in a mysterious manner (one without death, one by death but without ordinary burial), each had endured a supernatural forty-day fast, and each had communed with God on a holy mountain — they now appear in glorified form to confer with the Lord on the very subject (His coming 'departure,' Luke ix. 31) that had been the center of all their own prophetic witness, symbolically yielding up their delegated, now-expiring authority into His hands. Alford insists on the full historical reality of the event — confirmed by precise concurrence among all three Synoptic accounts, an allusion in John i. 14, and Peter's own direct eyewitness testimony at 2 Pet. i. 16–18.

μεθ' ἡμέρας ἕξ (vs. Luke's 'about eight days') — likely one count inclusive, the other not, or one precise and one a round approximation. Alford argues the event itself probably occurred at night: Luke says our Lord went up specifically to pray, which He characteristically did at night; the disciples are described as having stayed awake through the whole event (implying they would otherwise have been asleep, i.e., it was their normal sleeping hours); and they did not descend until 'the next day' (Luke ix. 37). The mountain's location is uncertain — probably not Tabor (likely topped by a fortified town at the time) but more probably one of the heights near the lake, possibly Hermon.
17:2: 2. μετεμορφώθη = Luke's 'the appearance of His face became different'; the radiant whiteness of His garments (Mark: whiter than any launderer on earth could bleach them) suggests an inner light shining through, not merely an external illumination.
17:3: 3. No need to speculate how the disciples recognized Moses and Elijah by name — the recognition may simply have been immediate and intuitive (against Olshausen's suggestion that it came from later explanation by our Lord, which Peter's exclamation in the next verse, made *during* the vision, rules out). Luke adds that the two spoke with Him of His coming 'departure' (ἔξοδος) to be accomplished at Jerusalem.
17:4: 4. Luke notes the disciples had been asleep but were now fully awake throughout this event (distinguishing it explicitly from a mere dream-vision), and that Peter's remark came as the two visitors were beginning to depart; both Mark and Luke add that Peter did not know what he was saying — Mark explains, 'for they were greatly afraid.' Alford rejects Meyer/Paulus's reading of Peter's words as merely practical ('how fortunate we happen to be here') — the phrase 'it is good for us to be here' will not bear that flattening; Peter's offer was likely prompted by the painful recent announcement of the Passion, freshly recalled by Moses' and Elijah's own conversation on that very subject.
17:5: 5. The cloud overshadowed 'them' — our Lord, Moses, and Elijah; Luke notes the disciples' fear specifically arose as the three entered the cloud, while the disciples themselves remained outside it, since the voice is said to come 'out of' the cloud. The command 'hear him,' paired with the simultaneous disappearance of the two heavenly visitors, symbolically signals that God, who had formerly spoken through the Prophets, now speaks definitively through His Son.
17:9: 9. ὅραμα implies no unreality — it is used interchangeably with 'what they had seen' in Mark and Luke (cf. similarly the term's use in Num. xxiv. 3, 4). Luke confirms the imposed silence by noting that 'in those days' they told no one anything of what they had seen.
17:10: 10. The question arose precisely because they had just watched Elijah withdraw before their eyes and were told to keep silent about it: if this was not 'the coming of Elijah,' was he yet to come? If it was, why so brief and so secret?
17:11: 11, 12. See note at ch. xi. 14. Our Lord here speaks plainly of a future, distinct fulfillment using the very wording of Malachi's prophecy (iv. 6): the partial fulfillment already accomplished in John the Baptist (forerunning Christ's first coming, in 'the spirit and power of Elijah') does not exhaust, but rather anticipates, a fuller, more literal fulfillment of the same prophecy still to come before the Lord's final, second coming.
17:14: vv. 14–21. Healing of a Demon-Possessed Boy. Mark ix. 14–29 (much fuller); Luke ix. 37–42. This occurred the next day, with our Lord finding the scribes disputing with the remaining disciples.
17:15: 15. He was an only son (Luke ix. 38); the demon had also deprived him of speech (Mark ix. 17).
17:17: 17. Bengel notes the disciples are sharply included within the rebuke directed at 'this faithless generation' — though Alford notes this is not entirely certain, given how closely the phrase is linked to the wider address.
17:19: 19. This question, per Mark, was asked privately in the house.
17:20: 20, 21. A vivid hyperbolic figure for faith's power, contrasted with the disciples' present 'little-faith.'
17:22: vv. 22, 23. Our Lord's Second Announcement of His Death and Resurrection. Mark ix. 30–32; Luke ix. 43–45. This followed immediately on the healing miracle (Mark ix. 30); our Lord now traveled through Galilee privately, specifically in order to teach His disciples this truth more fully and directly, continuing what He had begun at ch. xvi. 21.
17:24: vv. 24–27. The Temple Tax, and the Coin in the Fish's Mouth (peculiar to Matthew). This annual half-shekel tax (the δίδραχμον), required of every Jewish male twenty years and older for the Temple's upkeep (cf. Exod. xxx. 13), connects naturally with this chapter's larger theme of establishing Jesus as the true Son of God. It is not entirely clear from the text whether payment was strictly compulsory.
17:25: 25, 26. The entire force of our Lord's argument depends on this being understood as a *divinely* instituted tax, paid for God's own house: if sons of a king are exempt from taxes paid to their own father, then He, the Son of God, owes nothing to the tax of His Father's house. Alford notes that several major ancient and modern commentators (Clement, Origen, Jerome, Augustine) badly missed this point by treating the payment as a merely civil, secular tax.
17:27: 27. ἵνα δὲ μὴ σκανδαλίσωμεν αὐτούς — though exempt by right, our Lord chooses to pay anyway rather than give needless offense, graciously including Peter in the payment though the distinction between them was not to be disclosed; the means is provided miraculously rather than from ordinary funds, in a way that recalls Peter to his own great confession (ch. xvi. 16), which his hasty answer to the collectors shows he had momentarily half-forgotten. Alford insists on the plain literal-historic sense of the miracle, rejecting both the rationalizing reading (that the fish was simply to be sold for money) as inconsistent with the narrative's wording, and any mythical reading as wholly inapplicable to gospel history. The στατήρ = four drachmae, the exact sum required; ἀντί reflects that the tax was originally a ransom-payment for each person (Exod. xxx. 12); 'me and thee,' not 'us,' since Peter's relation to the tax and Christ's were on entirely different footings.
18:1: vv. 1–35. Discourse on the Greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven. Mark ix. 33–50; Luke ix. 46–50. Mark clarifies that this arose from a dispute among the disciples over who would be greatest — likely sparked by the recent special preference shown to Peter, James, and John, and by the mention of the kingdom at ch. xvi. 19, 28.
18:2: 2. Per Mark ix. 36, our Lord first set the child in the midst, then took it into His arms — possibly drawing the disciples' attention to its ready trust and submission as the very lesson intended.
18:3: 3. στραφῆτε = 'repent,' carrying also the sense of turning back from the very course just begun — namely, ambitious rivalry; without this change they would not merely fail to be pre-eminent but would not even be admitted into the kingdom at all.
18:4: 4. Valla's apt distinction: 'this little child does not humble himself, but simply *is* humble' — we are called not to imitate a child's literal innocence but to choose, by deliberate will, the same freedom from self-seeking ambition that is natural to a child.
18:5: 5. Having held up the child as a pattern of humility, our Lord now turns to the honor in which 'children' — both actual and spiritual — are held in His kingdom; receiving 'in my name' is equivalent to serving with Christian love, as belonging to Christ Himself (cf. ch. xxv. 40).
18:6: 6. The verbs κρεμασθῇ and καταποντισθῇ may carry their strict aorist sense ('it were better that a millstone had already been hung... and he already drowned, before...') though Alford notes this reading is uncertain — the aorist may simply denote a complete act without strict temporal precision. ὀνικός — the larger millstone turned by a donkey, as opposed to a smaller handmill stone — drowning with a heavy stone was an attested form of capital punishment among both Romans (cf. Suetonius on Augustus) and others, though Alford notes its Jewish use is disputed (Jerome affirms it, De Wette denies it).
18:7: 7. Stier suggests Judas — who would later take offense at the anointing at Bethany — may be in view as 'the man by whom the offense comes,' though the saying's general application is plain regardless.
18:8: 8, 9. The logical connection: 'if you wish to avoid being that man on whom the woe falls, then cut off every occasion of offense in yourself first.' These warnings extend the principle of ch. v. 29, 30 to a wider scope. τὸ πῦρ τὸ αἰώνιον occurs here for the first time in the Gospel.
18:10:
10. From this verse Matthew departs from Mark's parallel and stands alone. Alford insists the 'little ones' here are not merely (or even primarily) literal children but all the spiritually humble and newly-reborn within the kingdom — those furthest removed from worldly notions of 'greatness,' the very opposite of the ambitious rivalry that began this discourse; καταφρονήσητε specifically denotes the contempt that competitive ambition naturally breeds toward those too humble or weak to compete for status. Literal children are included as the natural, visible type of this spiritual humility, and the whole discourse, Alford suggests, carries a constant undertone bearing on infant baptism and the standing of baptized children within the covenant community.

On 'their angels always behold the Father's face': Alford rejects readings that evade the plain sense (e.g. taking 'angels' as 'departed spirits,' a meaning the word never bears); Scripture elsewhere clearly teaches that angels minister to God's children generally (Ps. xxxiv. 7; xci. 11; Heb. i. 14), and this verse confirms that a particular, individually-assigned order of guardianship is part of that ministry — high-ranking angels specifically charged with the care of the humble and meek.
18:11: [11.] (Bracketed as textually uncertain, likely a later insertion harmonizing with Luke xix. 10.) If genuine, it connects the angels' guardianship to the Son of Man's own saving mission: Stier's vivid image — 'here is Jacob's ladder planted before our eyes: beneath are the little ones, then their angels, then the Son of Man in heaven... and above Him again the Father Himself.'
18:12: 12, 13. Cf. the fuller parallel at Luke xv. 4–6, and Ezek. xxxiv. 6, 11, 12. ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη belongs grammatically to 'leaving' (the ninety-nine), not to 'going' — the preposition of motion captures the image of the flock having wandered and scattered over the mountains.
18:14: 14. This verse identifies the Son (the Good Shepherd of ver. 11–13) as the one accomplishing the Father's will in seeking the lost (cf. Ezek. xviii. 23; xxxiii. 11; 2 Pet. iii. 9); the implied inference is that whoever despises or causes one of these 'little ones' to stumble thereby acts directly against the Father's revealed will. Alford notes a subtle but deliberate shift: when the little ones' dignity is being asserted (ver. 10), it is 'my Father'; when a motive for the disciples' own conscience is being urged (ver. 14), it becomes 'your Father.'
18:15: vv. 15–20. The Method of Dealing with an Offending Brother, and the Authority of the Christian Assembly. 15. This applies specifically to personal offense against oneself, requiring private confrontation, with the offended party taking the initiative rather than waiting for an apology. The full stop belongs after 'alone,' against Fritzsche/Olshausen's proposed alternative punctuation, which Alford judges contrary to N.T. usage.
18:16: 16. The first step seeks private reconciliation; the second (taking one or two more) still aims, ideally, at quiet resolution, but also secures sufficient legal witness should the matter proceed further (cf. Deut. xix. 15; John viii. 17) — Paul's language at 2 Cor. xiii. 1 likely echoes this very saying.
18:17: 17. παρακούσῃ — a stronger word than mere 'not hearing,' implying real obstinacy. ἐκκλησίᾳ, by what follows (vv. 19, 20, which extend this power to any small gathered group of believers), cannot mean 'the Church' in any centralized, hierarchical sense — Alford states bluntly that 'nothing could be further from the spirit of our Lord's command than proceedings in what were oddly enough called "ecclesiastical" courts.' ἔστω σοι ὥσπερ ὁ ἐθνικὸς καὶ ὁ τελώνης — treated as an outsider, yet still, per 1 Cor. v. 11 and 2 Cor. ii. 6, 7, never with hatred.
18:18: 18. A reassertion, in wider and more general form, of the grant first given specifically to Peter (ch. xvi. 19) — here extended to the whole community of believers, not Peter alone, as the first foundation stone of a much larger building.
18:19: 19. A genuine grammatical instance of attraction — 'παντὸς πράγματος' is best understood as 'anything whatsoever,' referring to the complete, wholehearted unity of faith that itself could hardly exist except in conformity with the divine will (a condition apparently misunderstood, Alford notes, by James and John at Mark x. 35).
18:20: 20. A generalization of 'ἐκκλησία' and the powers conferred on it, making the promise independent of any particular form of church government or ceremony, and standing as a permanent rebuke to all pretensions of exclusive, hierarchical 'catholicism.' ἐκεῖ εἰμὶ ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῶν refers to the presence of Christ's Spirit and power (cf. ch. xxviii. 20).
18:21: vv. 21–35. Reply to Peter's Question on the Limits of Forgiveness; the Parable of the Unforgiving Servant. Cf. Luke xvii. 3, 4. The standing Rabbinic rule limited forgiveness to three offenses; the figure 'seven times' echoes Prov. xxiv. 16. Our Lord's answer ('seventy times seven,' not 'seventy-seven') likely alludes pointedly to Lamech's boast of vengeance at Gen. iv. 24 — Chrysostom: 'not naming a fixed number here, but the unlimited, continual, and perpetual.'
18:23: 23, 24. The 'servants' here are ministers or high officials, not literal slaves (their being 'brought' to the king, ver. 25, makes that clear) — in Oriental court language even great ministers of state were habitually styled the king's 'servants.' Trench helpfully compares the staggering scale of the debt (10,000 talents) to other biblical sums — far exceeding even the gold used for the entire tabernacle (29 talents) or the tribute Hezekiah owed Assyria (30 talents) — making clear the debt is meant to represent something utterly beyond any private person's power to repay.
18:25: 25. The image of selling the debtor and his family draws on Oriental despotic practice rather than strict Mosaic law (which permitted such servitude but tempered it by the Jubilee release) — the imprisonment and 'tormentors' of vv. 30, 34 likewise have no place in Jewish law as such, confirming the parable's broader, non-technical frame of reference.
18:26: 26. Trench reads the servant's desperate promise ('I will pay you everything') simply as the extravagant, half-coherent exclamation of someone in the grip of extreme terror, ready to promise impossible things — 'even mountains of gold' — rather than (per Luther's reading) the voice of a more deliberate, self-righteous bargaining instinct.
18:28: 28. The trivial sum owed by the fellow-servant (a hundred denarii, a tiny fraction of the first debt) is meant precisely to illustrate how insignificant any offense against a fellow human being is compared to the immensity of our debt to God. Chrysostom: 'he did not even remember the words by which he himself had just been saved... but driven by greed, cruelty, and resentment, became fiercer than any wild beast, throttling his fellow-servant.'
18:31: 31, 32. The fellow-servants 'were grieved' while the lord 'was angry' — Alford notes this distinction is deliberate: grief, not anger, is the properly Christian response to sin in others, since all men are themselves sinners; these grieving fellow-servants represent God's people interceding against injustice and oppression in the world.
18:34: 34. τοῖς βασανισταῖς — not mere ordinary jailers but tormentors proper, intensifying the severity of the punishment beyond simple imprisonment.
18:35: 35. The parable's solemn closing application: divine forgiveness already received is not unconditional in its ongoing effect — it demands, and is itself the ground for, a forgiving spirit toward others; withholding forgiveness 'from the heart' (not merely outwardly) toward a brother places the unforgiving person back under the very judgment from which he had been released. Alford notes the deliberate solemnity of 'my Father' here rather than the gentler 'your Father' of ch. vi. 14, 15.
19:1: vv. 1, 2. Transition to the Region beyond Jordan. Mark x. 1–12. Likely the journey alluded to at John x. 40; if so, a considerable interval has elapsed since ch. xviii. τὰ ὅρια τῆς Ἰουδαίας πέραν τοῦ Ἰορδάνου forms one continuous description — Bethany beyond Jordan, on the very confines of Judæa.
19:3: vv. 3–12. Reply to the Pharisees' Question Concerning Divorce. This was a live dispute between the rival schools of Hillel (permitting divorce for any cause, from Deut. xxiv. 1) and Shammai (restricting it to adultery alone) — and, De Wette notes, a delicate question to raise precisely in the territory of Herod Antipas, whose own marriage was under this very cloud.
19:4: 4–6. Alford highlights several features of our Lord's argument: (1) He treats the Genesis creation account as straightforward historical fact, grounding His argument in its literal wording; (2) He cites Gen. i and ii together as one continuous narrative, against critics who treat them as separate, inconsistent sources; (3) He attributes to the Creator Himself words actually spoken by Adam (Gen. ii. 24) — meaning these were understood as prophetically inspired utterance, since the relationships described did not yet exist when Adam spoke them (cf. Augustine: 'God spoke through man what man, prophesying, foretold'); (4) the argument's logical force rests on the original unity of male and female in Adam before Eve's creation — Gen. i. 27 says God made 'them' male and female (not 'a man and a woman'), implying the two were originally one, so that their reunion in marriage restores, rather than merely creates, that underlying unity.
19:5: 5. Stier observes that the essential bond of marriage is not (though it ought to be) unity of spirit and soul, but the more fundamental, unbreakable fact of being 'one flesh' for the duration of earthly life — a unity ended only by death, which is precisely why remarriage after a spouse's death involves no real violation of that prior union.
19:7: 7–9. The Pharisees imagine Moses' permission of divorce (Deut. xxiv. 1) overturns our Lord's argument by treating that permission as a positive command (note the deliberate contrast between ἐνετείλατο, 'commanded,' in their question and ἐπέτρεψεν, 'permitted,' in His answer) — but it was a concession to human hardness of heart, not a return to the original created order. Only πορνεία itself, which already breaks the marriage bond in substance, can rightly dissolve it formally. Alford notes the careful, deliberately restrictive grammar of ἀπολελυμένην (without the article) in both this passage and ch. v. 32, which logically confines the prohibition on remarriage to the case of a woman divorced *for some cause other than* πορνεία — a grammatical nicety Alford says even Bishop Wordsworth had missed.
19:10: 10. αἰτία here means not the ground for divorce just discussed, nor the man's situation with his wife, but the underlying rationale and principle of the marriage relationship itself: the disciples, startled by the strictness of this teaching, conclude that the trials of marriage under such a stringent rule might outweigh its benefits. This exchange is peculiar to Matthew.
19:11: 11, 12. τὸν λόγον τοῦτον refers back to the disciples' own remark ('it is not expedient to marry'). Our Lord identifies three groups for whom celibacy is fitting: those incapable of marriage by nature, those prevented by external compulsion, and those who voluntarily forgo it 'for the kingdom of heaven's sake' (i.e. for more effective service, as Paul, cf. 1 Cor. vii. 26) — Alford stresses this is explicitly framed as a *permission*, not a command, and implies no inherent superiority of the celibate over the married state; he cites Neander (himself unmarried) approvingly on this point, and notes that the parable of the talents, with its severe condemnation of burying one's talent for safety, argues against any general preference for celibacy as such.
19:13: vv. 13–15. The Bringing of Children to Jesus. Mark x. 13–16; Luke xviii. 15–17. The natural connection with the preceding discourse on marriage suggests this episode followed closely on further remarks (now lost to us) possibly touching the fruit of marriage.
19:16: vv. 16–30. The Rich Young Man. Mark x. 17–31; Luke xviii. 18–30. From Luke we learn he was a ruler; from Mark, that he ran eagerly to Jesus. Alford reads his spirit as one of admiring but shallow enthusiasm for Jesus as an exceptionally virtuous teacher, seeking some single great work of merit to secure eternal life — a spirit our Lord corrects by pointing him to the one true Good and the path of obedient holiness. Alford notes this passage is a textbook case of how later scribes 'smoothed' apparent discrepancies between the Synoptic accounts by harmonizing one Gospel's wording to another's.
19:18: 18, 19. De Wette rightly notes that our Lord's listing of the commandments is meant to draw out the young man's underlying self-righteousness, already perceived; only the commandments of the 'second table' (concerning neighbor) are named here, the first table having already been implicitly addressed in the preceding remark about 'the Good.' Mark adds 'do not defraud,' likely standing for the tenth commandment.
19:20: 20. Alford stresses this young man was no hypocrite or Pharisee — he spoke earnestly and genuinely believed he had kept the commandments; Mark notes Jesus, looking on him, loved him, recognizing a real nobility and openness in him quite unlike the calculated posturing of the Pharisees and scribes.
19:21: 21, 22. Our Lord takes him entirely at his own word — per Mark and Luke's fuller account, 'one thing thou lackest': granting the young man's claim to have kept the commandments, this is the missing capstone. Stier notes this command specifically tests his observance of the *first* commandment of the *first* table (loving God above all else) — a test by which, given the result, he stands convicted of having broken it after all.
19:24: 24. Alford firmly rejects the proposed softening of κάμηλος ('camel') into a supposed word for 'rope' or 'cable' — a reading invented, he judges, purely to escape the saying's deliberately startling force; he compares Talmudic proverbial hyperboles about an elephant passing through a needle's eye (cf. similarly ch. xxiii. 24, 'straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel'). The very point of the image is to express the greatest conceivable human impossibility, in order to magnify all the more the divine grace capable of overcoming even that.
19:25: 25. τίς — not 'what rich man' but simply 'who, then' — a question made more urgent by the disciples' own continuing expectation of a temporal Messianic kingdom, in which the wealthy would naturally seem best positioned to participate.
19:26: 26. ἐμβλέψας — our Lord's deliberate, searching look adds weight to the following saying, reaching as it does into spiritual truths the disciples could not yet fully grasp. παρά in both clauses carries the sense 'in the estimation of, with' (a rare N.T. usage of the preposition, paralleled only at John xix. 25).
19:27: 27. Peter, speaking for the disciples, recalls the promised 'treasure in heaven' offered to the young man and asks after their own reward, having actually done what the young man would not — Alford notes that 'all' which the disciples left was not, in every case, a trivial sacrifice (the sons of Zebedee had hired servants, Mark i. 20; Matthew/Levi could host a great feast) — but whatever its objective size, it was genuinely *their* all.
19:28: 28–30. Alford admires the simple truthfulness of our Lord's reply: He neither denies the validity of the disciples' question nor inflates their sacrifice, but promises a real, proportionate future reward (thrones of judgment over the twelve tribes at the renewal of all things) alongside the broader promise extended to anyone who makes a comparable sacrifice for His name's sake.
20:1:
ch. xx. 1–16. The Parable of the Laborers in the Vineyard (peculiar to Matthew). Bound by γάρ directly to the close of ch. xix and Peter's question 'what shall we have?' Alford reads its central point as: the Kingdom of God is of grace, not of debt — those called first and laboring longest have no greater claim on God than those called last, yet to all the covenant promise is fulfilled in full. Its primary application is to the Apostles themselves, warning against any spirit of supposing their early call and long labor entitles them to something supereminent over those called later (cf. 1 Cor. xv. 8–11); its secondary applications extend nationally (Jews called first, Gentiles later) and individually (those called early in life vs. late) to any case where comparative claims of priority, talent, or advantage might tempt the 'first' to pride.

On the μισθός ('reward, wages'): Alford firmly rejects Stier's reading of it as merely 'the promise of this present life,' insisting instead it is eternal life itself — God Himself (John xvii. 3) — held out, as Scripture regularly does, in covenant 'wage' language even though given wholly of free grace (cf. ver. 14). This reading, properly understood, in no way implies a flat, undifferentiated equality among the saved: rather, the grumblers' own un-Christian spirit disqualifies them from truly enjoying what is, formally, still given to them (Gregory the Great: 'no one who grumbles receives the kingdom of heaven; no one who receives it is able to grumble').
20:2: 2. The denarius was the standard daily wage of a Roman soldier under Tiberius — generous pay for a day's common labor.
20:3: 3, 4. The third hour (roughly 9 a.m.) was when the marketplace was at its fullest — Stier: 'the marketplace of the world is set against the vineyard of the Kingdom of God: the greatest man of business in worldly affairs is a mere idle bystander if he has not yet entered the true work that alone is worth anything.' No fixed wage is stipulated for these later laborers, only 'whatever is right' — likely understood, in each case, as the proportionate fraction of the full day's denarius.
20:8: 8. By Mosaic law (Deut. xxiv. 15) a hired servant's wages were due before nightfall.
20:10: 10. Alford rejects Greswell's proposed historical parallel from Josephus (regarding temple-rebuilding wages) as resting on a misreading of the Greek; he also notes the practical absurdity such a payment-rule would actually produce (it would *discourage*, not encourage, longer labor).
20:13: 13, 14. ἑταῖρε ('friend') takes on a more solemn, ominous coloring in light of its later uses — addressed to the wedding guest without the garment (ch. xxii. 12) and to Judas himself (ch. xxvi. 50).
20:16: 16. The 'first' are last in payment order, yet first in the sense of receiving full proportionate reward undiminished by a complaining spirit; the closing clause ('many are called, few chosen') explains how this can be — among the many called into the vineyard, some, through grumbling and otherwise disgracing their calling, will forfeit their place among the truly 'elect' despite their early, prominent calling.
20:17: vv. 17–19. The Third, Fullest Announcement of His Sufferings and Death. Mark x. 32–34; Luke xviii. 31–34. This version adds, uniquely among the Synoptics at this point, the explicit mention of crucifixion specifically.
20:20: vv. 20–28. The Ambitious Request of the Mother of the Sons of Zebedee. Mark x. 35–45 (where the brothers themselves, not their mother, make the request — Alford treats this as one of the common, unremarkable variations between a fact stated 'through oneself' and 'through another,' the two accounts converging exactly when Christ's answer addresses the two Apostles directly, ver. 22). Their mother was Salome, who had followed Jesus from Galilee and later witnessed the crucifixion (Mark xv. 40); Alford suggests the brothers directed the request through her, remembering the earlier rebuke for their previous contention over precedence.
20:21: 21. Seats nearest the throne were positions of highest honor in ancient royal court protocol (cf. Josephus on Saul's court). John had his accustomed place close to the Lord (John xiii. 23); James was one of the inner Three. Both were called 'Boanerges,' sons of thunder (Mark iii. 17), and, like the other disciples at this point, still expected the kingdom to appear immediately (Luke xix. 11).
20:22: 22. One of the two brothers would later actually see the Lord crucified between two thieves, on His right and left — Alford notes how bitterly ironic this ambitious request must have seemed in retrospect. Luther: 'the flesh always seeks to be glorified before it is crucified, exalted before it is abased.' The 'cup' signifies inward, spiritual suffering akin to Gethsemane; the added 'baptism' (in Mark's parallel) the outward trial and persecution to come.
20:23: 23. One brother (James) was indeed the first apostle to 'drink the cup' of martyrdom (Acts xii. 1, 2); the other (John) had, of all the Twelve, the longest subsequent experience of trouble and persecution.
20:24: 24. The ten react with indignation, evidently sharing the same underlying ambition the two brothers had simply voiced first.
20:25: 25. The two parallel verbs (κατακυριεύουσιν, κατεξουσιάζουσιν), both compounded with κατά, deliberately emphasize subjugation and domination — the pattern of worldly, Gentile rule that is to have no place among the disciples.
20:26: 26–28. 'Greatest... first' refers to status in the life to come; in the present, the path to it is to be servant and slave of all. λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν is a plain, direct statement of the sacrificial, substitutionary nature of Christ's death. Alford notes carefully that no theological weight should be placed on 'many' rather than 'all' here — the two terms simply reflect, respectively, the subjective and objective dimensions of the same redemption: Christ died for *all* objectively, while *many* (an innumerable multitude) will be those subjectively saved by that death in the end.
20:29:
vv. 29–34. Healing of (Two) Blind Men near Jericho. Mark x. 46–52; Luke xviii. 35–43. Alford treats the differing details among the three accounts (Mark and Luke name only one blind man, Bartimæus; Luke places the healing on entering Jericho rather than leaving it) not as discrepancies to be artificially harmonized but as honest, independent testimonies to the same underlying event, arising from each Evangelist's distinct sources — he sharply criticizes Greswell's proposed harmonization (two separate healings, conflated by Matthew) as itself impugning Matthew's honesty far more seriously than the supposed discrepancy ever could.

Jericho — about 18 Roman miles northeast of Jerusalem, a fertile oasis amid barren limestone hills, famous for palms and balsam, rebuilt under a curse (Josh. vi. 26) fulfilled when Hiel fortified it in Ahab's day (1 Kings xvi. 34), later embellished by Herod the Great, who built a palace there.
21:1:
vv. 1–17. The Triumphal Entry, and the Cleansing of the Temple. Mark xi. 1–11, 15; Luke xix. 29–44; John xii. 12–36. Reconciling the four accounts' minor differences, Alford proposes that our Lord's first arrival in Jerusalem (after a stop at Bethany) was effectively private — He went to the Temple, 'looked round on all things' (Mark xi. 11) and noted the abuses to be corrected, then returned to Bethany for the evening, the supper, and the anointing; the triumphal entry proper, the weeping over the city, and the cleansing of the Temple all then took place on the following day, with the cursing of the fig tree occurring early that same morning while still leaving Bethany.

Βηθφαγή = 'house of figs,' a suburb closer to Jerusalem than Bethany, of which no trace now remains.
21:2: 2, 3. Mark and Luke mention only the colt ('whereon never man sat'); John has a different word, 'a young donkey.' ὁ κύριος χρείαν ἔχει — most likely a general announcement to the owners that the animals were needed for God's service, possibly even implying Messianic claim ('the King Messiah'); the two disciples sent were perhaps Peter and John (cf. Mark xiv. 13; Luke xxii. 8).
21:4: 4. Alford's standard formula for fulfilled prophecy (cf. ch. i. 22): spoken with reference to the divine plan, not the disciples' own conscious intention at the time — John xii. 16 explicitly states this connection only occurred to them later, after Christ's glorification.
21:5: 5. The citation (Zech. ix. 9) is freely rendered, combined with Isa. lxii. 11.
21:6: 6, 7. Our Lord rode the colt itself (per Mark and Luke), with the mother accompanying alongside in the manner prophets were traditionally attended on such journeys. Alford insists the action was entirely deliberate on Christ's part — a solemn, public fulfillment of Messianic prophecy and a formal avowal of His mission, not any concession to popular expectations of a purely temporal kingship — and suggests this occurred on the very day the Passover lamb was being formally set apart for sacrifice, adding a typological resonance to the timing.
21:8: 8, 9. Spreading garments in the road was a recognized mark of royal honor (cf. 2 Kings ix. 13). ὡσαννά — from Ps. cxviii. 25 ('save now, we pray'), originally a cry of supplication that became conventionally one of acclamation, here followed by the dative and 'in the highest,' meaning 'may this be ratified in heaven too!' ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου belongs grammatically with 'he who comes,' forming a distinct Messianic title.
21:12: 12, 13. Alford insists this cleansing is wholly distinct from the earlier one recorded in John ii — too gross a chronological error to attribute to either careful Evangelist if the two were really the same event; the Synoptic Gospels' near-total silence on Jerusalem events prior to this final journey (their narrative being almost exclusively Galilean) explains why they simply omit the earlier cleansing altogether. The court in question was the Court of the Gentiles; the money-changing trade had likely arisen only after the Exile, when Jewish law (Exod. xxx. 13) required the half-shekel offering to be paid in proper currency rather than foreign coin, necessitating exchange for pilgrims from abroad. Doves were the prescribed substitute offering for the poor (Lev. v. 7; xii. 8).
21:13: Stier notes the citation from Jeremiah ('den of robbers') deliberately connects this scene with the charge of bloodshed in Jer. vii — Luther translates it Mördergrube, 'murderers' den.'
21:14: 14–16. The children's cry of 'Hosanna to the Son of David' within the Temple itself fixes this episode, in Alford's reading, to the very day of the triumphal entry. Ps. viii (cited here in answer to the priests' indignation) is frequently applied to Christ elsewhere in the N.T. (1 Cor. xv. 27; Heb. ii. 6; Eph. i. 22) — Alford notes the broader principle that the outward, historical fulfillment of such prophecies is often itself only a type of their deeper, ongoing spiritual fulfillment.
21:17: 17. If taken literally of the village itself (rather than the wider district including part of the Mount of Olives, cf. Luke xxi. 37), this would be the second night spent at Bethany — Alford prefers this literal reading, with the practice of overnighting on the Mount of Olives itself beginning only the following night.
21:18: vv. 18–22. The Cursing of the Barren Fig Tree. Mark xi. 12–14, 20–26 (Luke omits this). The cursing actually occurred the previous morning, with the withering only now noticed; Matthew compresses the two stages into one continuous account. Alford insists the miracle is wholly symbolic and parabolic: the fig tree represents the Jewish nation — full of the leafy show of religious profession, yet fruitless — and, by extension, hypocrites of every age; he rejects De Wette's objection that no explicit parabolic framing appears in the narrative, noting the same is true of the Temple-cleansing and many other admittedly symbolic actions of our Lord.
21:19: 19. μίαν — 'a solitary fig tree' in that particular spot. Fig trees were commonly planted along roadsides, the dust being thought to aid fruit production by absorbing exuded sap.
21:21: 21, 22. This promise echoes ch. xvii. 20. Alford stresses that the truest, highest faith implied here — a will perfectly united with God's own — necessarily excludes any thought of arbitrary, self-willed exercise of power; such faith, by its very nature, only ever asks 'if it be expedient.' He directs readers to the important parallel addition at Mark xi. 25, 26 (on forgiveness as a condition of effective prayer).
21:23: vv. 23–32. Our Lord's Authority Questioned; His Reply; the Parable of the Two Sons. Mark xi. 27–33; Luke xx. 1–8. This marks the beginning of the final, more openly hostile series of confrontations and parables between Christ and the religious authorities, provoking them at last to seek His death. The delegation's question was an official one, with Sanhedrin authority to formally examine a self-proclaimed teacher/prophet (cf. their similar deputation to John, John i. 19).
21:25: 25, 26. τὸ βάπτισμα stands for John's whole office and teaching, of which baptism was simply the central, sealing rite. Their private deliberation, recorded nearly verbatim by all three Synoptists, was perhaps originally relayed by Nicodemus or Joseph of Arimathea, both members of the council. Our Lord's reply ('neither will I tell you') answers not their stated words ('we do not know') but their actual unspoken thought ('we are unwilling to say').
21:28: vv. 28–32. The Parable of the Two Sons (peculiar to Matthew), directly addressing the dilemma the leaders had just dodged regarding John. The first son represents open sinners — tax collectors and prostitutes — who outright refuse God's call but later genuinely repent and obey; the second represents the scribes and Pharisees, who respond with a respectful, even self-congratulatory 'I go, sir,' yet never actually obey (cf. ch. xxiii. 3, 'they say, and do not'). Alford notes no particular significance should be read into which son is called 'first' versus 'second' (a detail subject to much textual confusion in transmission) — the parable simply marks the call as made 'likewise' to both.
21:31: 31. προάγουσιν — 'are going before you,' a plain statement of fact rather than a mere declaration of intent, chosen because it implies real hope, though not certainty, that the religious leaders might yet follow — the door of mercy not yet finally closed to them (cf. John xii. 35; Luke xxiii. 34).
21:32: 32. ὁδὸς δικαιοσύνης — not merely God's commandments generally but, more simply here, the path of repentance (cf. Noah called 'a preacher of righteousness,' 2 Pet. ii. 5, in a similar context). μετεμελήθητε ὕστερον deliberately echoes the same phrase from the parable (ver. 29), fastening the application directly onto the hearers.
21:33: vv. 33–46. The Parable of the Wicked Husbandmen. Mark xii. 1–12; Luke xx. 9–19. Closely tied to Isa. v. 1 ff., deliberately echoing that prophecy's own vocabulary (the fence, the winepress vat, the tower) as an explicit application of it to the Jews of His own day. The tenant arrangement reflects a common leasing practice in which rent was paid in kind (produce) rather than money.
21:34: 34–36. The repeated sendings of servants need not be pressed for individual precision — they collectively express the fullness and patience of God's warnings across the prophetic era (cf. Neh. ix. 26; Heb. xi. 36–38), while the husbandmen's escalating violence traces Israel's increasing rebellion against successive prophets.
21:37: 37. Our Lord depicts the Father in deeply human terms of deliberation ('what shall I do?' — Luke's parallel) to express His gracious willingness to try every possible means to bring sinners to repentance. Stier notes this verse forms the real, direct answer to the leaders' original question in ver. 23 about the source of Christ's authority — the Son here appears not yet in His redeeming office but specifically as the final messenger demanding the fruit owed to God.
21:38: 38. Alford notes a striking parallel with Joseph's brothers' words in Gen. xxxvii (LXX), almost certainly an intentional allusion by our Lord to that deeply typological history of rejection followed by exaltation. This very resolve had, in fact, already been formally taken by the council (cf. John xi. 53, immediately following Caiaphas's unwitting prophecy) — so that, Alford notes, from this point the parable shifts from prophecy into a description of events already underway.
21:39: 39. Understood both of Christ's being formally handed over to Gentile judgment and, quite literally, of crucifixion outside the city walls (cf. Heb. xiii. 11, 12).
21:40: 40, 41. Alford weighs whether it was the crowd (per Luke's framing, 'in the hearing of the people') or, as Trench and others suggest, the Pharisees themselves (perhaps genuinely or pretendedly missing the parable's application to themselves) who pronounced this self-condemning verdict — leaning, from the emphatic Greek wordplay (κακοὺς κακῶς, 'evil men, evilly'), toward the former. Either way, it stands as a striking instance of unwitting self-judgment, paralleling ch. xxvii. 25 — the sinner's own conscience, even at the last moment, interposing to warn him before the fact, in a mysterious convergence of human free will and divine foreknowledge.
21:41: See 21:40. Alford notes that our Lord here deliberately identifies 'when the lord of the vineyard comes' with the coming destruction of Jerusalem — an important interpretive key, in his view, for rightly understanding the various 'comings' described throughout Christ's later prophetic discourses.
21:42: 42. A citation from the same triumphal Psalm (cxviii) from which the crowd's earlier 'Hosannas' were drawn (also cited messianically at Acts iv. 11; 1 Pet. ii. 6, 7). The builders correspond to the husbandmen of the parable; the 'cornerstone' image (further developed at Eph. ii. 20–22) signifies Christ uniting Jew and Gentile in one new structure.
21:43: 43. Our Lord now drops the parabolic veil and states the application directly: the 'vineyard' is now explicitly named 'the kingdom of God,' and the 'nation' to whom it is given is not the Gentiles generally but the true, faithful Church — the 'holy nation, people for God's own possession' of 1 Pet. ii. 9 (cf. Acts xv. 14).
21:44: 44. Combines Isa. viii. 14, 15 with Dan. ii. 44, identifying that 'stone' explicitly with the stone of Ps. cxviii — the whole power and kingdom of the Messiah summed up in His own person. Those who 'fall on the stone' (taking offense at it) are broken; those on whom it falls in judgment (per Daniel's image) are utterly crushed — Alford prefers this reading of λικμήσει ('shall grind to powder,' the result of the stone's fall) over Meyer's more literal 'shall winnow him like chaff,' which Alford judges introduces needless confusion into the image.
22:1: vv. 1–14. The Parable of the Marriage of the King's Son (peculiar to Matthew, though resembling the parable of the Great Supper in Luke xiv. 15–24, which Alford insists is a genuinely distinct parable, given different occasion, locality, and tone — there the refusal is merely courteous and the penalty merely exclusion; here the guests turn violent and are utterly destroyed, binding this parable closely to that of the wicked husbandmen just preceding and to this final, more hostile period of the ministry).
22:2: 2. The earlier householder is now explicitly a King; γάμοι need not denote a literal wedding specifically but any great royal celebration (cf. LXX usage at Esth. i. 5; ix. 22) — though here marriage imagery is clearly intended, the great marriage supper of the Son (cf. Rev. xix. 9), His full union with His Bride the Church in glory.
22:3: 3. These δοῦλοι are not the same servants as in the previous parable (the prophets) but a fresh set, belonging to the New Testament era proper — John the Baptist, the Twelve, and the Seventy, who summoned 'those already invited' (i.e. the Jewish people, long since invited by covenant and prophecy) to the kingdom already at hand; Christ Himself, in taking 'the form of a servant,' may be included here too, though His own invitation goes further still ('come unto me').
22:4: 4. A second, later stage of invitation: now all is ready, the sacrifice itself accomplished — likely corresponding to the apostolic and evangelistic preaching after the cross (cf. John vi. 51–59). Meyer's distinction is apt: ἄριστον is not the main evening feast but the noon meal that traditionally opened wedding festivities — fitting the parable's sense of these as foretastes of the ultimate feast the Church even now enjoys.
22:5: 5, 6. Two classes of refusal: the indifferent and self-absorbed (note the pointed 'his own field' — selfish preoccupation) and the openly violent persecutors — Alford connects the latter directly to the documented sufferings of Stephen, James the son of Zebedee, James the Just, and Paul at Jewish hands.
22:7: 7. Though the Gospel reached the Gentiles roughly forty years before Jerusalem's fall, the final, decisive rejection of the Jewish nation as such, and the formal substitution of the Gentiles, did not occur until that destruction — making the verse's placement here, before the third invitation, strictly accurate rather than premature. 'Their city,' not 'His' — a striking, deliberate shift within the parable itself (cf. similarly 'your house,' ch. xxiii. 38).
22:8: 8–10. διέξοδοι — the public squares and crossroads, places of general resort; Alford corrects De Wette and Meyer's claim that 'going out to the highways' implies leaving the already-destroyed city — it is not the city of the murderers that is meant here but the larger world in which the feast is held.
22:10: 10. πονηρούς τε καὶ ἀγαθούς — both openly bad and morally good alike are gathered (cf. the net of ch. xiii. 47, gathering 'of every kind'); this marks the close of the parable's first act and describes the actual present state of the visible Church, gathered indiscriminately from the whole world.
22:11: 11, 12. This second movement directly echoes Zeph. i. 7, 8 ('I will punish... all such as are clothed with strange apparel'). The king's coming to inspect the guests represents the final, separating judgment — though Alford, following Trench, notes this judgment is not exclusively the very last one; every sifting trial of the visible Church in some measure anticipates it. On the 'wedding garment': Alford is skeptical of leaning too heavily on the supposed Oriental custom of provided festal robes (judging the usual proof-texts unconvincing), and in any case insists the custom, even if real, is not the parable's real point — the garment represents Christ's own imputed and inherent righteousness, put on symbolically in baptism and really by living faith (Gal. iii. 26, 27), without which none can stand before God; this guest, presumably, presumed his own righteousness sufficient and so neglected to provide himself properly.
22:13: 13, 14. The διάκονοι here are not the same as the inviting δοῦλοι above but the angels (cf. ch. xiii. 41, 49). Alford prefers Meyer's reading of the binding of hands and feet (simply to render escape from the outer darkness impossible) over more fanciful symbolic readings. Verse 14 generalizes: this single guest stands for a whole class within the visible Church — seated as guests, yet lacking the wedding garment when the King at last appears.
22:15: vv. 15–22. The Question of Tribute to Caesar. Mark xii. 13–17; Luke xx. 20–26. On the Herodians, see ch. xvi. 6. The combined approach of these two normally hostile factions (Pharisees, theocratic opponents of Roman rule; Herodians, beneficiaries of Roman-installed power) was a calculated trap: a negative answer would make Him a target for Roman prosecution (cf. Luke xx. 20; xxiii. 2); an affirmative one would compromise Him with nationalist hopes of a temporal Messiah and deliverer.
22:17: 17. κῆνσος = Luke's φόρος, the Roman poll-tax levied since Judæa became a province.
22:18: 18–22. A Rabbinic saying, cited by Lightfoot and Wetstein: 'wherever any king's coinage is current, there that king is lord' — our Lord's answer convicts the questioners by the simple fact of their own use of Roman currency, already implying subjection. Alford reads the second clause ('render to God the things that are God's') as the deeper, governing principle that actually comprehends and grounds the first: obedience to Caesar is itself simply one application of the larger duty of obedience to God, from whom all power derives. Man himself, made in God's image (Gen. i. 27), is the true 'coin' that belongs wholly to God — the deepest implication of the saying reaching, as Alford notes, far beyond the immediate tax question, to the total self-surrender owed to God.
22:23: vv. 23–33. Reply to the Sadducees on the Resurrection. Mark xii. 18–27; Luke xx. 27–40. Per Acts xxiii. 8, the Sadducees denied resurrection, angels, and spirits — and so, by extension, the soul's immortality generally, not merely bodily resurrection; Alford notes our Lord's answer is aimed at both errors together. He also corrects the common misconception (held even by some on Jerome's authority) that the Sadducees accepted only the Pentateuch — in fact they accepted the Prophets too, rejecting only the oral tradition.
22:24: 24. Levirate marriage (Deut. xxv. 5): the firstborn son of such a union was legally registered as heir of the deceased brother, not the actual father.
22:29: 29, 30. Our Lord's rebuke targets two distinct failures: ignorance of Scripture (which itself implies resurrection, ver. 31) and ignorance of the power of God (which removes the supposed obstacle, ver. 30). On angels and the future state, Alford reads ὡς ἄγγελοι ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ εἰσιν not as 'they are in heaven, as angels are' but 'they exist [on earth, in their resurrection state] in the manner that angels exist in heaven [now]' — the risen are not thereby relocated to heaven, but are transformed into a comparable mode of existence.
22:31: 31–33. Our Lord deliberately appeals to Moses rather than the more explicit prophetic resurrection texts (Isa. xxvi. 19; Ezek. xxxvii; Dan. xii. 2) — since the Sadducees' own difficulty was constructed precisely from their narrower reliance on the Pentateuch as final authority, the proof is most telling drawn from that very source. Alford's reading of the argument's logic: God's covenant declaration 'I am the God of Abraham' necessarily implies the patriarchs' continuing existence as the other party to that covenant — an assertion that could not truthfully be made of beings who had simply ceased to exist. Stier (after Lavater) notes this stands as a weighty biblical witness against any doctrine of 'soul sleep' in the intermediate state.
22:34: vv. 34–40. The Great Commandment. Mark xii. 28–34 (in Mark's fuller account this questioner does not appear to ask with hostile intent, which Alford judges the more likely reading here too, since no possible answer could have been used to entrap Him either way). νομικός — a legal specialist in Mosaic law, a narrower term than the broader γραμματεύς.
22:36: 36. ποία ἐντολὴ μεγάλη — not 'which is *the* greatest commandment' but more precisely 'what *sort* of commandment counts as great' in the Law.
22:40: 40. On these two commandments 'hangs' the whole Law and the Prophets — the entire body of revealed duty understood as flowing from, and finding its coherence in, this twofold love.
22:41: vv. 41–46. Whose Son Is the Christ? Mark xii. 35–37; Luke xx. 41–44. Having answered every hostile question put to Him, our Lord now turns the tables, posing His own question to the assembled Pharisees — drawn from Ps. cx. 1, a psalm universally acknowledged messianic. If the Messiah is merely David's human descendant, how can David himself, speaking 'in the Spirit' (i.e. under prophetic inspiration), call him 'my Lord'? The conundrum is calculated to press the Pharisees toward the deeper truth their own scribes' narrowly nationalistic, merely-human conception of Messiah could not accommodate — that the Christ is not only David's son by human descent but David's Lord by a higher, divine nature, the very mystery the Sadducees' and Pharisees' combined questioning throughout this chapter has been circling without grasping. The silencing of all His opponents that follows ('no one was able to answer Him a word, nor did anyone dare from that day to ask Him any more questions') marks the formal close of this whole sequence of public confrontations.
23:1: ch. xxiii. Denunciation of the Scribes and Pharisees (peculiar to Matthew, though much of the matter recurs scattered through Luke xi and xiii). Alford holds this was delivered as a single connected discourse on this one occasion, in these final days of the ministry — bearing many resemblances to the Sermon on the Mount, and standing as the solemn close of Christ's public teaching just as that sermon was its opening. It divides naturally into three parts: (1) introductory description of the Scribes and Pharisees, contrasted with the spirit required of Christ's disciples (vv. 1–12); (2) the solemn series of denunciations ('woes') against their hypocrisy (vv. 13–33); (3) the concluding, mournful farewell to Jerusalem and the Temple (vv. 34–39).
23:2: 2. 'Moses' seat' is the office of judge and lawgiver of the people; the principle: insofar as the scribes and Pharisees genuinely enforce Moses' own law, obey them — but do not imitate their conduct. ἐκάθισαν should not be read as implying blame in itself — it simply states the fact of their position; vv. 8, 10 below, however, do extend the warning to their claim of authoritative leadership as such, declaring that among Christians no one is to occupy 'the seat of Christ.'
23:3: 3. The οὖν is significant: 'because they sit in Moses' seat... do all that they, as his successors, command out of his actual law' — a careful distinction between their legitimate teaching as expounders of Moses and the frivolous human traditions added on top of it (condemned later in the chapter). ποιήσατε (aorist, occasional action) vs. τηρεῖτε (present, habitual rule of life) marks a deliberate grammatical distinction.
23:4: 4. The 'heavy burdens' are not, as commonly misread (even by Olshausen), human traditions specifically, but rather the *severity of the law itself*, which they impose on others while not observing it themselves (cf. Rom. ii. 21–23) — corresponding to the 'weightier matters of the law' at ver. 23. The law's irksomeness was not inherent to it rightly understood, but was manufactured by these men's rigid, letter-bound legalism: 'they spent all their effort urging and expanding the rites' (Grotius).
23:5: 5–7. Whatever they do is done from a single motive: to be seen. φυλακτήρια ('phylacteries') were strips of parchment inscribed with Scripture passages (Exod. xiii. 1–10, 11–16; Deut. vi. 4–9; xi. 13–21), worn on the forehead and left arm — apparently not in use until after the Exile, and so called because regarded as charms; their use arose from an overliteral reading of Exod. xiii. 9 and Deut. vi. 8, 9.
23:8: 8–10. The prohibition targets the *love of* such titles and any claim to dominion over others' faith — to be understood in spirit, not bound to the bare letter (Paul himself calls Timothy 'my son,' 1 Tim. i. 2). On 'call no man your father': Alford notes wryly how poorly the letter of this command has historically been kept by 'he who of all heads of sects has most notably violated this whole command... while calling himself servus servorum Dei' (an unmistakable jab at the papacy). Alford suggests 'the Teacher' (ver. 10) most likely refers not to Christ but to the Holy Spirit (cf. John xiv. 26) — left unnamed here since that promise had so far been given only privately to the disciples — so that, properly understood, the Trinity itself is declared here as the sole Father, Master, and Teacher of Christians, all of whom stand as equal brothers before God.
23:12: 12. This oft-repeated saying here points not only to the universal pattern of God's dealings but to the imminent, specific humiliation of these proud Pharisees — strikingly paralleled at Ezek. xxi. 26, 27.
23:13: 14. First Woe. (The textually disputed verse on devouring widows' houses, found in some manuscripts here as ver. 13 or 14, is bracketed by Alford as a likely interpolation from Mark xii. 40/Luke xx. 47.) In the parallel saying at Luke xi. 52, 'ye have taken away the key of knowledge' — the key being not access *to* knowledge but the true, simple interpretation of Scripture itself, which would have admitted both themselves and others into the kingdom by leading to the recognition of the One the Scriptures testify of; instead, by their perverse interpretations, they shut the door in people's faces (cf. John ix. 24 for a vivid instance).
23:15: 15. Second Woe. Not the godfearing Gentiles who simply attended synagogue worship, but the formally converted 'proselytes of righteousness' who, persuaded by Pharisaic teachers, took on the whole burden of Jewish law and ritual — rare converts, and, Alford observes dryly, all the better for human nature that they were rare, since what such teaching produced was 'a disciple of hypocrisy merely — neither a sincere heathen nor a sincere Jew — doubly a child of hell, condemned by the religion he had left, condemned again by that which he had taken.'
23:16: 16–22. Third Woe. Our Lord, having forbidden all oaths whatsoever to His own disciples (ch. v. 34), here uses the very same underlying logic to expose the absurdity and self-serving casuistry of the Pharisees' graded system of binding and non-binding oaths — since, by that same logic, every oath, traced to its root, really is an oath by God Himself, the ultimate source of holiness in every object invoked.
23:21: 21. κατοικήσαντι (aorist, 'who took up residence') rather than the present 'who dwells': Alford, following Meyer, reads this not as implying God's presence had since departed the Temple, but simply referring to the single definite historical act of God's taking possession of the Temple as His dwelling at Solomon's dedication.
23:23: 23, 24. Fourth Woe. It was disputed whether Lev. xxvii. 30 (tithing) extended to every smallest garden herb, but the Pharisees, in their excessive rigor over externals, stretched it to cover even this, while neglecting the law's truly weighty matters — Alford connects 'judgment, mercy, and faith' directly to Micah vi. 8's 'do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with God.' The point is not that minute observance should be abandoned, but that it must never come at the expense of, or substitute for, the weightier matters.
23:24: 24. 'Straining out the gnat' reflects an actual, attested Jewish practice (paralleled even today, Alford notes, among Buddhists in Ceylon and India) of carefully filtering wine to avoid swallowing ritually unclean insects per Lev. xi. The English 'strain at a gnat' (vs. the earlier 'strain out a gnat') Alford judges a deliberate, not erroneous, translation choice — 'strain [the wine] at [the occurrence of] a gnat.' The camel is paired with the gnat both for its enormous contrasting size and because it too was a ritually unclean animal.
23:25: 25, 26. Fifth Woe. This woe rests on a typical rather than strictly literal practice — Alford notes γέμουσιν ἐξ means 'are full of' (not 'filled by'), a Hebraistic construction. The point of ver. 26: 'that its exterior may not merely *appear* but truly *become* clean' — genuine purity cannot be merely external while the interior remains corrupt (Bengel: 'otherwise that outward cleanness is no cleanness at all').
23:27: 27, 28. Sixth Woe. The Jews annually whitewashed grave-sites (on the 15th of Adar) so that passersby would not unknowingly incur ritual defilement by walking over them (cf. Num. xix. 16) — a vivid, deliberately chosen image: 'your heart is not a temple of the living God but a grave of pestilent corruption... your religion is but whitewash, hardly skin-deep.'
23:29: 29–33. Seventh Woe. The guilt of these present Pharisees, as the last in a long line of such hypocrites and persecutors, forms the substance of the final woe: by the very act of building and decorating the prophets' tombs while disavowing their fathers' guilt, they unwittingly identify themselves as that same fathers' true heirs (cf. Luke xi. 47, 48) — Stier: 'instead of the penitent confession, "we have sinned, we and our fathers," this last and worst generation vainly protests its innocence of guilt it is, even now, busy completing.' πληρώσατε is imperative: 'go on, then, and fill up the measure of your fathers' sin' — and ver. 33 nearly repeats John the Baptist's own opening rebuke (ch. iii. 7), marking these closing words as the Lord's final answer to a generation that has remained entirely unmoved by the whole intervening ministry of repentance-preaching.
23:34: vv. 34–39. The Closing Lament over Jerusalem. Christ speaks here as Head of His Church, of those He is about to send out (the Apostles, Stephen and similar Spirit-filled witnesses, Apollos and Paul) — not, Alford insists, including Himself among those sent (against Olshausen), since the verse anticipates persecutions of Christian teachers still future at the time of speaking, well documented in the apostolic era (cf. Eusebius's account, via Hegesippus, of the crucifixion of Symeon son of Clopas under Trajan).
23:35: 35. ὅπως here means strictly 'in order that,' not merely 'in such a way that.' On the much-disputed identity of 'Zacharias son of Barachias': Alford rules out the later Zacharias mentioned by Josephus (an event still future relative to our Lord's actual speaking) and is skeptical of Origen's tradition identifying him with John the Baptist's father; he judges the most likely reference is Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, murdered in the Temple court (2 Chron. xxiv. 21), of whose innocent blood the Jews had a saying that it was never washed away until the Temple itself burned at the Babylonian captivity — noting that 'son of Barachiah' does not appear in the parallel saying at Luke xi. 51 and may be a later scribal insertion confusing this Zechariah with the prophet Zechariah, son of Berechiah (Zech. i. 1).
23:36: See note at ch. xxiv. 34 for Alford's wider discussion of 'this generation.' The Jews, standing at the very center of God's historical dealings with humanity, became, in rejecting His messengers, vessels of wrath in a peculiarly concentrated, representative sense — Abel's blood is cited as the opening instance not because it is chronologically nearest but because, like Zechariah's, it is explicitly recorded as crying out for vindication (cf. Gen. iv. 10).
23:37: 37–39. These words had already been spoken once before, at Luke xiii. 34 — Alford reads their recurrence here not as evidence of displacement or interpolation (against Wieseler) but as the natural repetition of a uniquely solemn utterance, its sound still 'dwelling on the mind of the narrator.' The lament gives way to a final, double-edged pronouncement: Jerusalem's house — the Temple itself — is now declared 'desolate,' abandoned by its rightful Inhabitant; and the people will not see Him again 'until' they themselves one day acclaim Him in the very words of Ps. cxviii, the same Hosanna-cry of the triumphal entry — a delayed but not finally foreclosed hope.
24:1: vv. 1, 2. The disciples point out the buildings of the temple. Jesus has just pronounced Jerusalem's house "left desolate" (23:38); now, departing from the temple for the last time, He is shewn its magnificence by the disciples — perhaps to suggest the question how such buildings could be given over to desolation. Alford notes the irony: they admire what He has just condemned.
24:2: 2. Christ's reply is an explicit, literal prophecy: not one stone shall be left upon another. This was fulfilled with extraordinary completeness in the burning and razing of the temple by Titus's soldiers in A.D. 70 (Josephus, B. J. vii. 1. 1), even against the express wish of Titus himself to preserve it.
24:3: vv. 3–28. The disciples' question, and the discourse on the signs preceding the end. On the Mount of Olives, over against the temple, the disciples ask a compound question — conflating, as Jews naturally would, the destruction of the temple with the παρουσία (coming) of Christ and the end of the age (συντέλεια τοῦ αἰῶνος), not distinguishing what to them seemed inseparable. Alford's governing principle for the whole discourse is that our Lord's answer maintains a designed indefiniteness, blending the near and far horizons — the overthrow of Jerusalem standing as a type and earnest of the final judgment — so that the lesser subject (the city's fall) is treated as a foreground image which is gradually "swallowed up" by the greater (the final coming), the transition occurring about v. 28/29.
24:4: 4, 5. The first sign: deception by false christs — fulfilled in part by impostors before A.D. 70 (Josephus mentions several, e.g. Theudas, the Egyptian, B. J. ii. 13), but with a further and fuller reference to the latter days.
24:6: 6, 7. Wars, rumours of wars, nation against nation: not yet the end, but the beginning. Historically answered, in the near term, by the troubled reign of Claudius and the agitations preceding the Jewish war; famines are recorded under Claudius (Acts 11:28, and Josephus, Antt. xx. 2. 5, on the famine relieved by Queen Helena); earthquakes are likewise attested in this period at Crete, Smyrna, Miletus, and elsewhere by Tacitus and other historians.
24:8: 8. These are but the beginning of travail-pangs (ἀρχὴ ὠδίνων) — the first throes of a far greater and longer process, not its consummation.
24:9: 9, 10. Persecution and hatred of all nations, and the falling away of many, betraying one another. Fulfilled in the experience of the apostolic church (cf. Acts, and the Neronian persecution, A.D. 64), yet pointing onward to the apostasy of the latter days.
24:11: 11, 12. False prophets, and the waxing cold of love through the abounding of lawlessness — again a near and a far fulfilment together.
24:13: 13. Endurance to the end — the great practical lesson running through the whole discourse, applicable alike to the individual believer's death and to the church's final trial.
24:14: 14. The gospel preached in the whole world (οἰκουμένῃ) for a witness to all nations, and then the end shall come. Alford takes this both of the apostolic preaching, attested as remarkably widespread before A.D. 70 (Col. 1:6, 23; Rom. 10:18), and, in its fuller sense, of a final universal proclamation immediately preceding the last end.
24:15: vv. 15, 16. The abomination of desolation, and the flight to the mountains. The reference is to Daniel 9:27; 12:11, the language of the prophecy intentionally retained ("whoso readeth, let him understand") to direct readers back to the original. Alford weighs the patristic and historical interpretations: most identify the sign with the planting of the Roman standards (the "eagles") in the holy place, or with Titus's army surrounding the city, as Luke's parallel (21:20) more plainly states ("Jerusalem compassed with armies"). Alford, however, argues for an internal Jewish fulfilment as well: the desecration of the temple by the Zealots themselves shortly before the final siege, who took possession of the sanctuary, defiled it with bloodshed, and set up a mock high priest, Phannias, by lot, in contempt of all law and order (Josephus, B. J. iv. 3. 6–8). On this view Luke's sign is the external, visible token (the besieging armies) and Matthew's the internal, specifically Jewish token (the profanation within), both marking, from different vantage points, the same approaching catastrophe — the moment at which flight was no longer optional but final and immediate.
24:17: vv. 17–22. The urgency of the flight, and the great tribulation. He on the housetop must not even descend to remove goods from his house; he in the field must not turn back for his cloak — such was the suddenness with which the catastrophe was to fall once begun, and indeed Josephus records the flight of the Christian community of Jerusalem to Pella in Peræa shortly before the final investment, having been forewarned (Eusebius, H.E. iii. 5, citing an oracle).
24:19: 19, 20. Woe to those with child or nursing infants in those days — and pray that the flight be not in winter nor on a sabbath, when both the weather and the Jewish-Christians' own scruples about a sabbath day's journey would hinder a sudden departure. This minute, specifically Jewish detail (peculiar to Matthew) shews how literally and immediately the first stage of the prophecy was meant to be heeded by the Jewish church, which continued to observe the law up to the destruction of Jerusalem.
24:21: 21, 22. Tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of the world, nor ever shall be — language which Alford takes as having a real, terrible, near fulfilment in the horrors of the siege (cf. Deut. 28:49–57, literally fulfilled in the case of Mary of Peræa, who in the extremity of famine ate her own child, as related by Josephus, B. J. vi. 3. 4), while still pointing forward to a yet future and final tribulation of which the former was the type. Were the days not shortened, Alford notes (following Josephus's own narrative), no flesh would have survived; he traces several providential causes that did in fact shorten the siege — the unfinished state of Jerusalem's fortifications under Herod Agrippa (halted by order of Claudius), the Jews' own factional self-destruction, the burning of their corn magazines just before Titus's arrival, and the suddenness of the Roman assault.
24:23: vv. 23–26. Renewed warning against false christs and false prophets. Restated for emphasis, with the addition that they shall shew great signs and wonders, so as to deceive, if possible, even the elect — a warning whose primary historical reference (cf. Josephus, B. J. ii. 13.4, on impostors leading the people into the wilderness with promises of deliverance, e.g. before Acts 21:38) is exceeded by its ultimate reference to the seductions of the last days (2 Thess. 2:9–12).
24:27: 27. The coming of the Son of Man shall be like lightning, flashing from east to west — sudden, universal, and unmistakable, in contrast to the secret, localized claims of the false christs just warned against.
24:28: 28. Wheresoever the carcase is, there the vultures (ἀετοί, properly the vultur percnopterus, not eagles, and certainly not a covert allusion to the Roman military standards, an interpretation Alford firmly rejects) will be gathered. The primary reference is to the doomed body of Jerusalem and the gathering of the agents of judgment upon it; the ultimate reference, to the whole corrupted world at the final judgment. This verse marks the hinge of the discourse, after which (vv. 29ff.) the language ceases to bear even an indirect reference to A.D. 70 and addresses the final, personal coming of Christ directly.
24:29: vv. 29–31. The cosmic signs, and the coming of the Son of Man in glory. "Immediately after the tribulation of those days" — Alford explains that εὐθέως here does not require strict chronological immediacy, but takes up the indefinite period of "the times of the Gentiles" (cf. Luke 21:24) during which Jerusalem is trodden down, until the fulness of the Gentiles comes in. The darkening of sun and moon and falling of stars is to be understood as a literal physical occurrence at the last day (as elsewhere in the prophets), while also serving as the time-honoured prophetic figure for the collapse of human society and authority — sun, moon and stars typifying respectively the Lord's own light, the reflected light of human knowledge, and the teachers and leaders of the church.
24:30: 30. The sign of the Son of Man in heaven, at which all the tribes of the earth shall mourn, and shall see Him coming on the clouds with power and great glory. Alford declines to identify the precise nature of the "sign" (rejecting both the view that the Son of Man is Himself the sign, and Wetstein's rationalizing notion that it refers merely to the smoke of burning Jerusalem), though noting the tradition, found widely among the Fathers, that it refers to the sign of the Cross appearing in the sky. This coming is identified with that of 1 Thess. 4:16–17 and Rev. 19:11ff — the Lord's coming to inaugurate His glorious reign — and is distinguished from the coming to final judgment described in 25:31.
24:31: 31. The angels gather the elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other, at the sound of a great trumpet — language echoed in 1 Thessalonians, though this is not, Alford notes, identical with the trumpet of the general resurrection (1 Cor. 15:52), except in so far as that resurrection is itself the first stage of this same gathering.
24:32: vv. 32–35. The parable of the fig tree, and the abiding of "this generation." As the budding of the fig tree announces summer, so the appearance of "all these things" announces that the coming is near, even at the doors. Alford sees a further allusion to the cursed, withered fig tree of ch. 21 — emblematic of the Jewish nation in its judicial unfruitfulness — so that its future putting forth of leaves symbolizes the eventual revival of that nation, of which the next verse speaks.
24:34: 34. "This generation (γενεά) shall not pass till all these things be fulfilled." Alford insists, against the rationalist critics who treat this verse as a failed prediction, that γενεά here does not mean the generation of Christ's contemporaries but, as demonstrably elsewhere in Hellenistic usage (e.g. 12:45; 23:36 read with 23:35; Luke 16:8), a race or family of people — i.e., the Jewish people, or race, which shall endure, unextinguished, until the complete fulfilment of all these prophecies, including the final coming. He stresses that the continued use of παρέρχομαι ("pass away") through vv. 34–35 ties the verse directly to the eternal endurance of Christ's words, not to a near-term deadline, and that the apostolic church continued, after the first Christian generation had indeed passed away, still to look for the Lord's coming.
24:35: 35. Heaven and earth shall pass away, but Christ's words shall never pass away — an assertion of the absolute permanence of His teaching, set deliberately alongside the preceding verse.
24:36: 36. Of that day and hour knows no one — not the angels, not even the Son, but the Father only. Alford insists this weighty statement of the Lord's voluntary self-limitation in His incarnate state must not be explained away (as some commentators attempt by saying merely that He does not disclose it to us); it belongs to the genuine humiliation in which the Son increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52) and learned obedience (Heb. 5:8).
24:37: vv. 37–39. The days of Noah. As in Noah's time men ate, drank, married, all unaware until the flood swept them all away, so shall the coming of the Son of Man be — sudden, amid the ordinary business and false security of life, the danger present even while men say "there is peace."
24:40: 40, 41. Two in the field, two grinding at the mill — one taken, one left. Alford takes this as referring neither to the secret flight of vv. 16–18 nor to the general judgment of 25:31 (where all are summoned together), but to the gathering of the elect at the Lord's coming to inaugurate the millennial reign (v. 31) — the taking and leaving describing the sudden, discriminating action of the angels amid ordinary daily occupations, the sexes mingling together in common life up to the very last.
24:42: vv. 42–44. Exhortation to watch, and the parable of the thief. Because the hour is unknown, the householder who does not know at what watch the thief comes must be ever ready, lest his house be broken into. So must the disciples be ready, for the Son of Man comes at an hour they do not expect.
24:45: vv. 45–47. The faithful and wise servant. Set over the household to give food in due season, and blessed if his lord finds him so doing at his coming — he shall be made ruler over all his lord's goods. Alford notes this parable had already been spoken substantially in Luke 12:42–46, our Lord repeating and gathering His teaching, as was natural, around recurring images in His final discourses.
24:48: vv. 48–51. The evil servant. The transition is from the good to the bad servant — or even from the good to the bad state of mind of the same servant — marked by the contemptuous demonstrative "that" (ἐκεῖνος). "My lord delays his coming" (χρονίζει) presupposes, Alford notes, that a real, possibly long delay was in view from the first — confirming that the discourse as a whole anticipates an extended interval before the final coming, not an imminent end within that generation in the narrow sense.
24:50: 50, 51. The lord comes in an hour the servant does not expect, and cuts him in two (διχοτομήσει — the ancient punishment of sawing or cutting asunder, cf. Dan. 2:5; Susanna 59), appointing him his portion with the hypocrites: there shall be the weeping and gnashing of teeth. Alford suggests the cutting asunder may carry a symbolic reference to the dreadful inward severing of conscience from practice that constitutes the self-torment of the condemned — the very mingling and confounding of which had made the sinner's double life tolerable to him in this world.
