25:1: vv. 1–13. The Parable of the Ten Virgins. Peculiar to Matthew. The ten virgins, all alike furnished with lamps and going out to meet the bridegroom, represent souls who have come out of the world into the Church and wait for the Lord's coming — not hypocrites with a dead faith, for all the lamps are genuinely burning at first. The lamps are the heart kindled with the flame of heavenly love; the oil vessels, kept separate from the lamps themselves, are the crucial element of the parable.
25:2: 2–4. The difference between the wise and the foolish is not in the lamp but in the provision of oil in the vessel — i.e., not in possessing the initial light of faith, but in seeking, through the appointed means of grace, an ongoing supply of the Spirit to feed and sustain it. The foolish presumed that a light once kindled would burn on of itself.
25:5: 5–7. All grew drowsy and slept, the bridegroom tarrying — Alford takes this simply of the universal weakness of human watchfulness, even in the holiest, rather than as a special sign of spiritual decline; the real difference between wise and foolish emerges only when the cry comes and the lamps must be trimmed (κοσμεῖν, by replenishing the oil and removing the charred wick).
25:8: 8, 9. "Our lamps are going out" — Alford stresses this means going out, not already extinguished: there was still some life in the foolish virgins' profession, but no reserve to sustain it. The wise virgins' refusal to share is not selfishness but plain fact: no one can supply another's lack of personal, inward provision of grace.
25:10: 10–12. The door is shut, and even the cry "Lord, Lord, open to us" meets the answer "I know you not." Alford carefully distinguishes this judgment from the final judgment of ch. 25:31ff: it is not said the foolish virgins could not have bought oil, only that it was too late for that opportunity — this scene corresponds, in the parable's individual application, to the readiness or unreadiness of the soul at the hour of death, prior to and distinct from the final judgment of all nations.
25:13: 13. "Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour" — the express moral of the parable, applicable to the individual believer's death as much as to the Lord's final coming.
25:14: vv. 14–30. The Parable of the Talents. Peculiar to Matthew (distinct from the similar but separate parable of the pounds in Luke 19:11–27, spoken on another occasion). Where the virgins illustrate the contemplative, inward readiness of the Christian life, the talents illustrate its active side and its corresponding danger: the foolish virgins fail from thinking their part too easy, the wicked servant from thinking his too hard.
25:15: 15. Each servant receives "according to his own ability" — Alford notes there is no inequity here, since each man's powers are themselves God's gift; in Luke's parallel parable all receive the same sum but produce different results, whereas here all in fact receive proportionately the same, since ability itself is the measure of the gift.
25:16: 16–18. The two faithful servants gain the full amount again — as much shall be required of each as has been given him; the third servant, by contrast, is not an active wrongdoer like the wicked servant of 24:48, but a hider of what was entrusted to him.
25:19: 19–23. "After a long time" (μετὰ πολὺν χρόνον) — Alford notes this again signals, as in 24:48 and 25:5, that a substantial interval was contemplated before the reckoning. This accounting, like the bridegroom's coming, belongs to the judgment of Christ's own servants at the beginning of the millennial reign, not the final judgment of all the world; it concerns a review of a past course of action, in contrast to the virgins' parable, which concerns a present state of preparedness. The faithful servant's words, "you delivered to me" and "I have gained besides them," disclaim self-credit, attributing the increase to his master's enabling. "Well done, good and faithful servant" — note it is faithfulness, not mere success or amount, that is commended; the reward of the servant of five talents and of two talents is identical, since both were equally faithful with what they had.
25:24: 24, 25. The third servant's excuse — that his master is a hard man, reaping where he did not sow — sets forth, Alford says, the perpetual human excuse of inability to keep God's commands made by those who never apply to the grace that would enable them; the excuse is self-convicting and false, and his pretended fear is belied by his own insolent speech in voicing it.
25:26: 26, 27. The master's reply takes up the servant's own words hypothetically, not concessively: it is not a true description of God, but an argument from the servant's own professed (and false) premise — "if thou really thought me such a hard master, all the more reason to have put my money to the bankers," thereby avoiding even the appearance of unfaithfulness.
25:28: 28–30. The talent is taken from him and given to the one who has ten — illustrating the general law of the Kingdom (cf. 13:12) that to him who has, more shall be given, and from him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away; a principle true even in nature, where a limb used grows strong and one disused grows weak. The casting of the useless servant into outer darkness again evokes the marriage supper from which he is excluded.
25:31: vv. 31–46. The Final Judgment of All Nations. Peculiar to Matthew. Alford marks this as a distinct and later scene from the two preceding parables: those concerned the judgment of Christians specifically, in connection with the first resurrection and the millennial Kingdom; this is the great, universal judgment of all the dead at the very end of that period, corresponding to Revelation 20:11–15. The precision of "when… then" in v. 31 signals both the indefiniteness of the time and the certainty that it will come.
25:32: 32, 33. "All the nations" gathered before Him are distinguished from the elect already gathered to Him in the earlier scenes — these are the rest of mankind, separated as a shepherd divides sheep from goats (cf. Ezek. 34:17), the sheep representing those described in Romans 2:7, 10, the goats those of Romans 2:8–9, where the same judgment according to works is described.
25:34: 34. Here, and here only, the Lord calls Himself "the King." Alford explains "the blessed of my Father" and the kingdom "prepared from the foundation of the world" as compatible with a judgment by works: the good these persons did was wrought in them by grace, even though, per v. 37, they themselves are unaware that it was done for and to Christ — their love, not the formal religious knowledge of having served Him, is what is commended (cf. notes at 25:40 on "the least of these my brethren").
25:35: vv. 35, 36. The works of mercy enumerated. Feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, welcoming the stranger (συνηγάγετε — receiving with hospitality, numbering them among one's own circle), clothing the naked, visiting the sick and imprisoned.
25:37: 37–40. The righteous answer, "When did we see you hungry…?" — a response which Alford (following Olshausen and Stier) takes as proof that these are not consciously the covenanted servants of Christ in the narrower sense; they did not know they were serving Him, in contrast to the faithful servants of the previous parable who knowingly served their master. It is the love itself, not conscious service rendered to Christ by name, that is commended — "for in as much as you did it to one of the least of these my brethren, you did it to me." "My brethren" is taken not narrowly of the saints alone but of the wider family of mankind, fulfilling the promise to Abraham that in his seed all the nations of the earth should be blessed.
25:41: 41–43. The curse to those on the left is carefully distinguished by Alford from the blessing of v. 34: the kingdom was "prepared for you," but the everlasting fire was prepared originally for the devil and his angels, not for man — for there is, Alford insists, election to life in Scripture, but no corresponding doctrine of reprobation to death; a book of Life is spoken of, but no book of Death. Those who are condemned are condemned by their own choice to share the devil's fate, not by any original decree against them as such.
25:44: 44, 45. The condemned likewise protest their ignorance of having failed Christ — see note at 25:37.
25:46: 46. "Everlasting punishment" and "eternal life" are set as exact contraries, the same epithet (αἰώνιος) applied to both — Alford stresses that the life spoken of here is not bare existence (whose opposite would be annihilation) but blessedness and reward, of which punishment and misery are the true antagonists. Alford candidly notes, reflecting on the chapter as a whole in his third edition, that he held his prophetic interpretation of its three sections (the virgins, the talents, the judgment) with less confidence than formerly, while still regarding their correspondence with the sequence of last things in Revelation 20–21 as an indispensable guide, however tentatively held.
26:1: vv. 1, 2. Final announcement of the Passion, now close at hand. Having finished all these sayings, Jesus tells the disciples plainly that the Passover, now two days off, will coincide with His being delivered up to be crucified — a deliberate identification, Alford notes, of the Paschal sacrifice with His own, fixing the chronological anchor for the whole Passion narrative.
26:3: vv. 3–5. The conspiracy of the Jewish authorities. The chief priests, scribes, and elders gather at Caiaphas's palace and agree to take Jesus by guile, but not during the feast itself, lest there be an uproar among the people — a resolve providentially overturned, since the actual arrest did occur during the feast, occasioned by Judas's unforeseen offer.
26:6: vv. 6–13. The anointing at Bethany. Inserted here out of strict chronological order — it actually occurred six days before the Passover (John 12:1) — because of its connection to the application of Judas to the Sanhedrim that follows. Alford suggests the rebuke Judas received on this occasion (cf. John 12:4) helped precipitate his decision to betray Jesus, even though his name is not mentioned in Matthew's account of the anointing itself. Simon "the leper" was presumably a healed leper, since he could not otherwise host guests.
26:7: 7. The woman (Mary of Bethany, per John 12:3) pours costly ointment from an alabaster cruse upon His head (and, per John, His feet) as He reclines at table.
26:8: 8, 9. The disciples' indignation at the "waste" — though John specifies it was Judas who voiced this complaint, with others perhaps seconding it.
26:10: 10, 11. Jesus' rebuke: "she has wrought a good work upon me" — Alford notes Stier's observation that this is a stronger expression than merely "a good work," marking it a noble act of love to be commemorated to the end of time.
26:12: 12. "She did it to prepare me for burial" — Alford finds it hard to believe our Lord would have said this unless Mary's act had carried, even unconsciously, some genuine reference in her own mind to His approaching death, which all at the table must have sensed was near.
26:13: 13. The promise that this deed shall be told wherever the gospel is preached in the whole world — the only such promise of its kind in the Gospels, and, Alford observes, a striking indication that our Lord here explicitly anticipated the existence of a written gospel record, since only by writing could the deed's universal commemoration be secured.
26:14: vv. 14–16. The compact of Judas with the chief priests. Probably immediately following the Sanhedrim's meeting of v. 3. Alford gives an extended assessment of Judas's character: a man of practical business talent (hence his role as treasurer, John 12:6; 13:29), in whom the self-seeking element common to all the apostles was rooted more deeply and unchecked by the deeper spiritual susceptibility the others possessed; as our Lord's path diverged further from his worldly hopes, attachment curdled into disappointment, then aversion. The immediate triggers were probably the rebuke at Bethany, the bitter enmity of the authorities following the triumphal entry, and the renewed announcement of the Passion in v. 2. Alford concludes that sordid gain, achieved through the darkest treachery, was Judas's essential motive.
26:15: 15. Thirty pieces of silver — the price set in the law for a slave's life (Exod. 21:32), and the sum specified only by Matthew, deliberately echoing Zechariah 11:12–13.
26:17: vv. 17–19. Preparation for the Passover. Alford devotes extensive discussion to the famous chronological difficulty of reconciling the Synoptic Last Supper (on the evening beginning the 14th of Nisan, the ordinary time for the Passover) with John's Gospel, which seems clearly to place the crucifixion itself at the time the Passover lambs were being slain — implying the Last Supper preceded the legal Passover. He reviews and rejects in turn the proposed harmonizations (an anticipatory Passover; differing Jewish calendrical practices; a merely commemorative, non-sacrificial meal; Chrysostom's theory that the Sanhedrim themselves ate the Passover late out of bloodthirsty haste) as each either unsupported by evidence or contrary to the plain sense of one Gospel or another. He candidly states he has no solution of his own that fully satisfies him, while offering several considerations: that the meal was clearly treated by the Synoptics as a true Passover; that John's account, taken on its own terms, seems to exclude this; and that perhaps Luke 22:15–16 ("I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you... I will not eat it any more") hints at an anticipatory, non-customary character to the meal even within the Synoptic tradition itself.
26:18: 18. "Go into the city to a certain man" — as in the colt's preparation (21:2ff.) and the room for the Passover (Mark 14:13–15), this reflects not prior arrangement but our Lord's supernatural knowledge and command of circumstances. "My time is at hand" (ὁ καιρός μου) refers not to the feast in general but to His own approaching suffering.
26:20: vv. 20–25. Jesus announces His betrayer during the meal. A full Paschal company of thirteen, exceeding the minimum of ten required. Here too belong (per the other Gospels, not Matthew) the washing of the disciples' feet and the dividing of the first cup.
26:22: 22. Each disciple asks in turn, "Is it I, Lord?" — in John's fuller account, the actual inquiry was made by John himself at Peter's prompting.
26:23: 23. "He who dips his hand with me in the dish" — does not single out Judas to the rest, since all were eating from the common dish; the indication was understood by Judas alone, or revealed to John alone by a separate sign (cf. John 13:26).
26:24: 24. "Woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed — good were it for that man if he had not been born" — the Son of Man goes as it is written of Him (the divine foreordination of the event), yet this does not lessen the betrayer's guilt or accountability.
26:25: 25. Judas's own question, "Is it I, Rabbi?" and Jesus' answer "Thou hast said" — Alford takes this, peculiar to Matthew, as representing in summary form what John relates in fuller, more precise detail: that Jesus privately and silently identified Judas to John alone by handing him the dipped sop, not as an open accusation before the whole company (cf. John 13:28, where even John says no one understood why Judas went out).
26:26: vv. 26–29. Institution of the Lord's Supper. Alford treats this at length as the foundation of a permanent ordinance, instituted in close connection with, yet transcending, the Passover meal then in progress; he draws the typological line from the Paschal lamb's blood (the sign protecting the household) to the blood of the new covenant, truly partaken by faith. On "this is my body," Alford insists on the precision of τοῦτο ("this" — the bread itself, not merely "this bread" or "this wine"), arguing for neither a bare symbolic nor a transubstantiating reading, but a real, spiritual identification grounded in Christ's own sustaining relation to all created and redeemed life (cf. John 6:51; Col. 1:17) — the literal sense undergirding and giving fitness to the higher spiritual and commemorative sense ("do this in remembrance of me").
26:27: 27. The cup likewise given to all to drink — Alford notes the emphatic πάντες ("all of you"), pointedly opposed to the later Roman practice of withholding the cup from the laity.
26:28: 28. "My blood of the new covenant, shed for many for the remission of sins" — Alford traces the typology from Exodus 24:8 ("the blood of the covenant") through to its fulfilment in Christ's blood, the once-for-all ἄφεσις ἁμαρτιῶν (remission of sins) of Hebrews 8–10 superseding the repeated, insufficient offerings of the old covenant. He closes the note by stating plainly that this exegesis is wholly incompatible with the doctrine of transubstantiation.
26:29: 29. "I will not drink of this fruit of the vine until I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom" — Alford reads this, with Thiersch, as giving the Sacrament not only a commemorative but a prophetic meaning, anticipating its consummation in the marriage supper of the Lamb.
26:30: vv. 30–35. Declaration that all would forsake Him; Peter's overconfidence. After the hymn (probably the latter portion of the Hallel, Psalms 115–118), they go out to the Mount of Olives — at this point, by John's account, the great discourses of John 14–17 were spoken.
26:31: 31. "All of you shall be offended (σκανδαλισθήσεσθε) because of me this night" — citing Zechariah 13:7, "Smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered," which Alford defends as a genuine messianic prophecy against Grotius's denial of the reference.
26:32: 32. The promise to go before them into Galilee after His resurrection — Alford rejects Schleiermacher's objection that this is improbable given the subsequent Jerusalem appearances, noting the threefold repetition of this same promise (cf. 28:7, 10, 16) makes a later interpolation highly unlikely.
26:33: 33, 34. Peter's vehement protest, and Christ's precise prediction of a threefold denial before the cock crows — Alford notes the very specificity and confidence of Peter's outburst ("though all men..., yet will I never...") betrays that this was not the first time his loyalty had been so strongly, and suspiciously, asserted (cf. Luke 22:31–34).
26:35: 35. Peter's further protestation, "Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee" — echoed by all the disciples; Mark's stronger phrase ("he spoke the more vehemently") confirms this was no isolated declaration.
26:36: vv. 36–46. The Agony in Gethsemane. Alford frames the whole episode as requiring the reader to hold firmly to the full reality of Christ's human nature, in all its abasement and weakness, in tension with the unshaken divine purpose and will, never for a moment overborne even amid the most extreme dread — the human will, troubled to the point of death, voluntarily and continuously submitted to the higher, divine Will at one with the Father's. Gethsemane ("oil press") lay at the foot of Olivet, across the Kedron from the city.
26:37: 37, 38. Peter, James, and John are taken further in, not chiefly as witnesses but as a human consolation to Jesus in this hour — "My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death" (περίλυπος, ἕως θανάτου), language Alford treats not as mere proverbial hyperbole, as it might be in human speech, but as bearing its fullest literal weight when spoken by the Lord: His soul, the seat of human affections, was crushed to the point that physical death itself would have followed had not strength been ministered to His frame from heaven.
26:39: 39. "Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." Alford takes the "cup" to mean not merely the immediate bodily anguish but the whole entirety of what was to follow — betrayal, trial, mocking, scourging, cross, and grave. He reads this passage as decisive refutation of the Monothelite heresy (which held only one will in Christ): the human will genuinely wills deliverance, yet is wholly and freely submitted to, and at one with, the divine will — there is no question of the Father's wrath resting on the Son as the cause of His suffering, only the deepest filial submission amid human anguish.
26:40: 40, 41. Finding the three asleep, Jesus rebukes Peter particularly (Mark's singular address) — the one who had pledged to go with Him to prison and death. "Watch and pray, that you enter not into temptation" — Alford distinguishes merely being tempted (unavoidable, even profitable, James 1:2) from "entering into" temptation with the will, deliberately entertaining it.
26:42: vv. 42–44. The second and third prayers. "If this cannot pass from me except I drink it, thy will be done" — a prayer of fuller self-resignation than the first, Alford suggests, reflecting the Lord's understanding (per John 11:42, that the Father always heard Him) that the continuance of the trial was itself the Father's answer.
26:45: 45, 46. "Sleep on now, and take your rest... it is enough; the hour is at hand" — Alford takes this as a genuine, not ironic, permission (in effect, "since you could not watch with me, you may rest now, for the crisis that makes further watching needful has come"), immediately followed by the call to rise and meet the approaching band.
26:47: vv. 47–56. The betrayal and arrest. The armed multitude accompanying Judas comprised, Alford suggests, a detachment of the Roman cohort garrisoned at Antonia, the temple officers, servants of the high priest, and possibly some of the chief priests and elders themselves, eager to ensure the arrest's success; the swords and "staves" (rough makeshift weapons, not formal clubs) were meant to suggest a dangerous insurrectionist was being apprehended.
26:49: 49. The kiss — Alford suggests this was not merely a gesture of false affection but functioned as a prearranged identifying sign for the benefit of the Roman soldiers present, who likely did not personally know Jesus and required such confirmation before acting under orders.
26:50: 50. "Friend, wherefore art thou come?" (ἐφ' ὃ πάρει) — Alford, following Euthymius and Meyer, reads this as an aposiopesis (a deliberately broken-off sentence): "Friend, there is no need of this pretence — do what you came to do," the actual command left suppressed, the whole remaining an appeal to Judas's conscience even at this last moment.
26:51: 51, 52. Peter (named explicitly only in John 18:10) strikes the high priest's servant Malchus with his sword; Jesus rebukes him — "all who take the sword shall perish by the sword," which Alford reads not as a reference to the Jews' fate under Rome but as a general, almost imperative declaration (echoing Gen. 9:6) condemning the private, self-willed taking up of God's reserved vengeance, here exemplified by Peter's rash act.
26:53: 53, 54. "Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?" — peculiar to Matthew, displaying, Alford says, both the Lord's majesty and His patience; the number twelve probably corresponds to the company present (the Lord and the eleven) rather than to the twelve apostles as such. "How then shall the scriptures be fulfilled, that thus it must be?" — His abstention from invoking such aid is itself a further mark of voluntary self-submission to the Father's will.
26:55: 55, 56. "Are you come out as against a robber, with swords and staves to take me? I sat daily teaching in the temple, and you laid no hold on me" — addressed, per Luke's more precise account, to the chief priests, temple captains, and elders specifically present. "All this was done that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled" — Alford judges this clause, despite Matthew's usual practice of citing a specific text, to belong to the substance of our Lord's own speech rather than to be the Evangelist's editorial comment, since Mark independently preserves an equivalent statement in Jesus' own words.
26:57: vv. 57–68. The hearing before Caiaphas. Alford notes (following John's fuller account) that a prior informal hearing before Annas, the de facto power behind the high priesthood, preceded this formal one before Caiaphas, the high priest of that particular year; this gathering, though it concludes with a unanimous verdict of guilt (v. 66), was not the formal, official condemnation, which occurred the following morning (Luke 22:66–71).
26:58: 58. Peter follows at a distance into the court (αὐλή) of the high priest's residence — the same building, Alford notes, that housed both Annas and Caiaphas, accounting for the apparent overlap in the denial narratives across the Gospels.
26:59: 59, 60. The Sanhedrim seeks false testimony but cannot find adequate or self-consistent witness — Alford reads this not as meaning they would have refused true testimony, but that they knew none could be found sufficient for their purpose.
26:61: 61. The two witnesses' charge — "I am able to destroy the temple of God, and build it in three days" — Alford notes the false witness consisted precisely in twisting the sense of Jesus' actual saying (cf. John 2:19) into a literal threat against the physical temple, a meaning which, per 27:63, even the authorities privately knew it did not bear.
26:62: 62, 63. Caiaphas presses Jesus to answer the charges; He remains silent, since any explanation would have required disclosing truths not fitting for that hour or audience. Caiaphas then places Him under solemn oath: "I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us whether thou be the Christ, the Son of God."
26:64: 64. "Thou hast said" — Alford suggests this affirmation may carry more weight than Mark's simple "I am," perhaps appealing to Caiaphas's own prior admissions (cf. John 11:49–51). Jesus adds the prophecy of His exaltation: "hereafter shall you see the Son of Man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven" — a declaration, Alford notes, that His glorification is reckoned by Christ Himself as beginning precisely at this moment of betrayal and condemnation (cf. John 13:31).
26:65: 65, 66. Caiaphas rends his garments, declaring blasphemy, and the council pronounces Him "guilty of death" — a preliminary judgment, not yet the formal sentence delivered the next morning.
26:67: 67, 68. The mockery and physical abuse that follow — per Luke's parallel, inflicted not by the Sanhedrim members themselves but by the guards holding Him in custody.
26:69: vv. 69–75. Peter's threefold denial. Alford gives an extended comparative table of the four Gospel accounts' differing details (who recognized Peter, in what words, in what order), concluding that the discrepancies are best explained not as inconsistencies but as marks of genuine, independent eyewitness testimony — multiple recognizers and repeated, vehement denials likely occurred on each of the three occasions, with each Evangelist independently preserving different details of the same underlying, complex scene. He explicitly declines to force the four accounts into a single harmonized sequence, regarding the attempt as both impossible and unprofitable, while affirming complete confidence in the truthfulness of all four as independent, complementary witnesses.
26:73: 73. "Surely thou also art one of them, for thy speech betrays thee" — a reference to the distinctive Galilean dialect, which could not properly pronounce certain Hebrew gutturals.
26:74: 74, 75. Peter's culminating denial, with cursing and swearing, followed immediately by the cock's crow and his memory of Christ's prediction — he goes out and weeps bitterly. Alford notes the motive for his departure (per Chrysostom) was so that his tears might not betray him further before the crowd.
27:1: vv. 1, 2. Jesus is led away to Pilate. A formal morning meeting of the Sanhedrim, ratifying the verdict of the night before, to devise how to bring about His death; He is then taken to Pilate, the Roman governor, since the Jews under Roman occupation lacked authority to carry out a capital sentence themselves.
27:3: vv. 3–10. The remorse and suicide of Judas. Peculiar to Matthew. Seeing Jesus condemned, Judas is overcome with remorse and returns the thirty pieces — Alford argues this was clearly the full price of betrayal, not mere earnest money, since by this point Judas would otherwise have collected the remainder. "I have sinned in that I have betrayed innocent blood" — his own confession, in the perfect tense, of an accomplished, deliberate act, telling against any theory that he never expected or intended Jesus' condemnation; Alford reaffirms his view (cf. 26:14) that Judas's motive throughout was sordid gain pursued through deliberate treachery.
27:5: 5. Judas casts the silver into the temple (ναός, the sanctuary itself, where only priests might enter) and hangs himself; on the differing account in Acts 1:18, see Alford's note there.
27:6: 6. The chief priests, citing precedent from Deuteronomy 23:18, refuse to put the "price of blood" into the temple treasury (corban).
27:7: 7, 8. The money instead purchases the potter's field as a burial ground for foreigners — called "the field of blood" to Matthew's own day, a detail Alford notes indicates a considerable interval had passed before this Gospel was written.
27:9: 9, 10. The citation attributed to "Jeremy the prophet" actually corresponds (loosely, and seemingly from memory) to Zechariah 11:12–13 — Alford treats this candidly as an imprecise citation rather than attempting strained harmonizations, comparing similar loose quotations elsewhere in the New Testament (e.g., Acts 7:4, 16; Mark 2:26), and judges this more honest than theories which suppose a deliberate, providential conflation of two prophets' names.
27:11: vv. 11–14. Jesus is examined by Pilate. "Art thou the King of the Jews?" — the formal charge against Him being that He called Himself Christ, a king. "Thou sayest" is, as at 26:64, a strong affirmative, not an evasive or doubtful answer.
27:12: 12–14. Jesus answers nothing to the further accusations of the chief priests and elders, to Pilate's astonishment — His silence is of a piece with His silence before Caiaphas, declining to dignify groundless or politically motivated charges with response.
27:15: vv. 15–26. Barabbas preferred to Jesus; He is delivered to be crucified. The custom of releasing one prisoner at the feast (κατὰ ἑορτήν, "feast by feast") is otherwise unattested in surviving records, though analogous customs are known elsewhere in antiquity (Alford cites Livy on the Roman Lectisternium). Barabbas ("son of his father") was a notorious prisoner, one of several murderers involved in an insurrection (cf. Mark 15:7).
27:17: 17, 18. Pilate, already aware (per v. 19 and his wife's message) of Jesus' character, offers the crowd the choice, knowing the charges against Jesus stemmed from envy.
27:19: 19. Pilate's wife (traditionally named Procla or Claudia Procula) sends word during the trial, having suffered "many things in a dream" because of Jesus, calling Him "that just man" — language showing she already recognized His character for purity and innocence.
27:20: 20, 21. The chief priests and elders persuade the crowd to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus — the agitation apparently occurring while Pilate was occupied with his wife's message.
27:22: 22. "What then shall I do with Jesus, called Christ?" "Let him be crucified" — crucifixion being both the standard Roman penalty for sedition and the outcome desired by Jesus' accusers out of hatred.
27:23: 23. "Why, what evil has he done?" — Pilate's question, introduced by an impassioned γάρ, conceding the crowd's position only to press them for a justifying reason they cannot supply, met only with increased clamor.
27:24: 24. Pilate washes his hands before the crowd — a gesture intelligible to Jews from Deuteronomy 21:6–9 as a sign of innocence of bloodguilt, though Alford notes the Greek idiom (ἀθῷος ἀπό) is itself slightly unusual, a concession to local custom rather than ordinary Greek usage. "I am innocent of the blood of this just person" — peculiar to Matthew, and indicating that he "prevailed nothing," not that his protest accomplished nothing for himself, but that his attempt to release Jesus failed.
27:25: 25. "His blood be on us, and on our children" — Alford takes this not narrowly as invoking a specific legal penalty but, more broadly, as the crowd's voluntary, fateful assumption of the guilt of an innocent man's death.
27:26: 26. Barabbas released; Jesus scourged and delivered to be crucified — scourging before crucifixion being the regular Roman practice; per John's fuller account, Pilate's final, unsuccessful attempt to release Jesus occurred after the scourging, not before it.
27:27: vv. 27–30. Jesus mocked by the soldiers. Taking place in the Praetorium (Herod's former palace, the Roman governor's residence), before the whole cohort — a scene Alford suggests may have reached the Evangelists through the testimony of the centurion or other soldiers later deeply affected by witnessing the crucifixion (cf. v. 54).
27:29: 29. The crown of thorns — Alford discusses at length the uncertainty over which plant was used, favoring some pliant, many-thorned shrub (perhaps a variety later identified by travelers in Palestine) rather than the rigid spina Christi sometimes proposed, since a true wreath required flexible branches. "Hail, King of the Jews" mocks the very charge that condemned Him.
27:31: vv. 31–34. He is led to crucifixion. Executions were customarily carried out outside the city or camp (cf. Heb. 13:11–13). Jesus had initially borne His own cross (John 19:17) before Simon of Cyrene was compelled (ἀγγαρεύω, the technical term for impressment into forced service, cf. 5:41) to carry it; Alford notes nothing further is reliably known of Simon beyond the likelihood that he became a known figure in the early church (cf. Mark 15:21).
27:33: 33. Golgotha, "place of a skull" — Alford weighs but does not fully endorse either of the chief explanations (an habitual place of execution littered with skulls, or a hill shaped like a skull), noting neither is wholly satisfactory, and discusses the unresolved question of the site's exact location relative to the traditional Holy Sepulchre.
27:34: 34. The drugged wine offered and refused — a customary stupefying drink given to those about to be executed, which Jesus declines after tasting it, demonstrating full conscious awareness in approaching His death. Alford notes Matthew's wording ("vinegar mingled with gall") echoes Psalm 69:21 more closely than Mark's plain narrative description ("wine mingled with myrrh"), an instance of Matthew's recurring tendency to color his narrative with the language of the prophecy being fulfilled.
27:35: vv. 35–38. He is crucified. Alford describes the mechanics of Roman crucifixion in some detail: an upright beam crossed by a transverse one, the condemned affixed by nails through the hands and (not invariably, but not rarely) the feet, the body's weight borne chiefly by a wooden support rather than the nails alone. The soldiers' division of His garments and casting of lots is related without the explicit citation of Psalm 22:18 found in some manuscripts, which Alford judges (with most modern critics) to be a later interpolation from John 19:24.
27:37: 37. The inscribed charge fixed above His head — Alford notes the differing wording recorded across the four Gospels is a clear, instructive example of the limits of strict verbal harmonization between independent, truthful accounts: one title existed, differing probably from all four reports, certainly from three of them.
27:39: vv. 39–44. He is mocked on the cross. Passers-by, the chief priests, scribes, and elders, and even the two crucified robbers join in the reproach — echoing the false charges of 26:61 (destroying the temple) and 26:64 (claiming divine sonship).
27:42: 42, 43. "He saved others, himself he cannot save" — the mockery's logic unconsciously affirms the very truth it intends to deny. The taunt "let him deliver him now, if he will have him" echoes Psalm 22:8 closely, though not identical to the Septuagint wording.
27:45: vv. 45–50. The supernatural darkness; the last words and death of Jesus. Darkness over the land from the sixth to the ninth hour — Alford insists this was no natural eclipse, since it was full moon at Passover, and was firmly attested by all three Synoptic accounts as well as patristic appeals to pagan testimony (Tertullian, Origen, Julius Africanus). He leaves open whether "all the land" should be taken with strict universality or understood of the region around Jerusalem specifically, while affirming the historical reality of the event itself is beyond reasonable doubt.
27:46: 46. "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani — My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Ps. 22:1, in the Aramaic Jesus actually spoke, not the Hebrew of the psalm text). Alford treats this with great care: Christ's inner consciousness of union with the Father remained complete and indestructible, yet was, like His holy will, capable of being obscured by the extremity of human pain and the direct confrontation of His soul with death as the wages of sin He bore but never committed — Gethsemane's conflict renewed at its furthest extremity. Yet even this cry retains, in the word "My God," the same essential union with the Father's will expressed in "not my will, but thine."
27:47: 47. The bystanders' mocking claim that He calls for Elijah — not a genuine misunderstanding (the Jewish hearers would have understood the Aramaic "Eli" perfectly well) but a deliberate further mockery.
27:48: 48. Vinegar offered on a reed in response to His cry "I thirst" (John 19:28) — Alford allows this may be a distinct incident from the earlier mocking offer of vinegar in Luke 23:36, occasioned now by genuine response to His physical state rather than mockery alone.
27:49: 49. "Let be, let us see whether Elijah will come to save him" — continued mockery while the vinegar is offered; Alford notes the verses appended in some manuscripts describing the spear-thrust (properly belonging to John 19:34, after Jesus' death) are a clear and identifiable later interpolation, mistakenly inserted here before the death narrative.
27:50: 50. Jesus cries again with a loud voice and yields up His spirit — Alford identifies this final cry with the "It is finished" of John 19:30 and "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit" of Luke 23:46, understanding the three accounts as together describing a single moment rather than separate utterances.
27:51: vv. 51–56. Signs following His death. The veil of the temple (the inner veil separating the holy of holies) is torn from top to bottom — Alford reads this as the great antitype of the Day of Atonement's typical access to God's presence, now genuinely opened to all through Christ's sacrifice as both victim and high priest (cf. Heb. 10:19–21), and firmly rebuts Schleiermacher's skepticism that the event could not have become known or that it lacks reference in Hebrews.
27:52: 52, 53. The earthquake, splitting of rocks, opening of tombs, and resurrection of "many bodies of the saints" who appeared in Jerusalem after Christ's own resurrection. Alford defends the full historicity of this passage against critics (notably Meyer) who accepted the earthquake but dismissed the resurrected saints as legendary accretion, arguing the whole scene is a single, coherent, symbolic-yet-real declaration that death's dominion was broken: the tombs opened at the moment of Christ's death, but — since He is "the firstfruits of them that slept" — the saints did not themselves rise until after His own resurrection.
27:54: 54. The centurion and those with him, having witnessed the earthquake and "those things that were done," declare in fear, "Truly this was the Son of God" — Alford insists the centurion used this in a genuinely Jewish theological sense, informed by what he had heard of the charges against Jesus (cf. v. 43; John 19:7), rejecting Meyer's suggestion that he meant only a pagan demigod, since no such loose pagan usage of the precise phrase can be shown.
27:55: 55, 56. The women who had followed Jesus from Galilee, watching from a distance — including Mary Magdalene (from Magdala, not to be confused with other Marys in the Gospels), Mary the mother of James and Joses (wife of Alphaeus/Clopas), and the mother of Zebedee's sons (Salome). Alford notes the absence of Mary the mother of Jesus from this list is explained by John's account (19:26–27) of her being led away by the beloved disciple immediately after the words "Behold thy mother."
27:57: vv. 57–61. Joseph of Arimathea begs and buries the body of Jesus. A rich man, a member of the Sanhedrim (per Mark and Luke) who had not consented to the council's verdict, and a disciple of Jesus — Alford notes the great courage and risk this open request to Pilate represented, occurring before sunset on the eve of an unusually solemn Sabbath.
27:59: 59. The body wrapped in clean linen — John adds the detail (not known to the Synoptic writers) of Nicodemus bringing a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes for the burial; Alford treats the partial, non-overlapping knowledge of different details among the various witnessing groups of disciples as wholly natural amid the haste and confusion of that evening.
27:60: 60. Laid in Joseph's own new tomb, hewn from the rock, with a great stone rolled to the door — Alford infers from the practical logic of the situation (haste before the Sabbath, the need for the tomb owner's consent) that Joseph's ownership, mentioned only by Matthew, best explains how an executed criminal's body could be laid in so honorable and private a resting place on such short notice.
27:61: 61. Mary Magdalene and "the other Mary" remain, sitting opposite the sepulchre, watching where He was laid — the same women who would return after the Sabbath to find the tomb empty.
27:62: vv. 62–66. The Jewish authorities obtain a guard for the sepulchre. Peculiar to Matthew. Alford carefully defends the historicity of this episode against the skepticism of Olshausen, Meyer, De Wette, and others, answering in turn each major objection raised: that the authorities could not have known of Jesus' resurrection prediction (the meaning may have been hidden from the disciples while the bare fact of the saying was not a secret, cf. John 2:19; Matt. 12:40); that the women were unaware of any guard (they were not present when it was set, the evening before, and had no reason to expect news of it before the third day); and that other sources (such as Gamaliel's reported uncertainty in Acts 5:39) do not corroborate it (not every Sanhedrist need have taken part in or known of every later step against Jesus). The request itself — "that man deceiver said, while he was yet alive, After three days I will rise again" — Alford notes shows that hatred is keener-sighted than love in grasping at a feared possibility the disciples themselves had not yet understood.
27:65: 65. "You have a guard (ἔχετε κουστωδίαν); go, make it as secure as you can" — Alford, after weighing whether ἔχετε is indicative ("you already have") or imperative ("take a guard"), inclines to the imperative reading, given that the guard subsequently reports to the chief priests rather than to Pilate (28:11), indicating it was placed under Sanhedrim, not Roman, authority.
27:66: 66. The tomb is made secure, sealing the stone and setting the watch — the seal likely a cord stretched across the stone and fastened at either end with sealing-clay, so that any tampering would be immediately evident.
28:1: vv. 1–10. Jesus, having risen, appears to the women. Alford prefaces the chapter by candidly abandoning any attempt to harmonize the resurrection narratives of the four Gospels into one continuous, reconciled sequence — he judges all such harmonies, however well-intentioned, to weaken rather than strengthen the evidence, which rests on the independent, unexceptionable testimony of separate witnesses; he regards John's account as generally the most precise where it overlaps with the others, without thereby excluding the value of the rest. "In the end of the sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week" — Alford works through the seeming tension between this phrase and the other Gospels' timing, concluding both the day and the dawning should be understood in their natural, not technical-Jewish, sense, in harmony with Mark, Luke, and John.
28:2: 2. The earthquake (σεισμός) here was not a general seismic event but specifically the shock accompanying the angel's descent and the rolling away of the stone — Alford stresses this did not coincide with the resurrection itself, which had already occurred; the stone was removed not to let Christ out, but to let the women and disciples in.
28:3: 3, 4. The angel's appearance "like lightning," his raiment "white as snow" — ἰδέα here means not his shape but his appearance, specifically his brightness. The guards, struck with terror, become "as dead men."
28:5: 5, 6. "Fear not ye" — emphatic, addressed to the women in contrast to the terrified guards. "He is not here, for he is risen, as he said" — Alford notes the angel's report fulfills Christ's own repeated predictions (16:21; 17:23).
28:7: 7. The promise of His appearing in Galilee, foretold already at 26:32 — Alford observes Matthew records only this one resurrection appearance (in Galilee), apparently in keeping with his practice of giving a general, summary account of each cycle of events rather than every individual detail; he does not thereby deny the Jerusalem appearances recorded by Luke and John.
28:8: 8. The women depart "with fear and great joy" — fear at what they had witnessed, joy at the good news they had heard (Euthymius).
28:9: 9. Jesus Himself meets the women; they take hold of His feet and worship Him — Alford cites Bengel's remark that before the Passion, those more remote from Him were often quicker to do Him homage than His own disciples.
28:10: 10. "Go tell my brethren" — the same term used to Mary Magdalene in John 20:17; Alford weighs whether this is the same appearance as John's but judges the evidence inconclusive, the available materials being admittedly fragmentary.
28:11: vv. 11–15. The Jewish authorities bribe the guards to give a false account of the resurrection. Peculiar to Matthew. The chief priests' secret council — Alford suggests this was likely an informal, off-the-books compact among the most hostile members of the Sanhedrim rather than a full official session, since others (perhaps Gamaliel among them) may well have withdrawn from any further proceedings against Jesus, just as Joseph of Arimathea had done earlier.
28:13: 13, 14. "Say that his disciples came by night and stole him away while we slept" — a self-refuting story, since sleeping guards could hardly testify to what happened while they slept; the bribe and promise of protection from Pilate's wrath if the matter "come to the governor's ears" reveal the cynicism of the cover-up.
28:15: 15. "This saying is commonly reported among the Jews until this day" — Alford cites Justin Martyr's Dialogue with Trypho as independent external confirmation that this very story (of the disciples stealing the body) was indeed circulated among Jews well into the second century.
28:16: vv. 16–20. Appearance of the Lord on a mountain in Galilee, and the Great Commission. The eleven go to the mountain Jesus had appointed — Alford notes this implies prior, unrecorded communications during the Galilean period, illustrating the admittedly fragmentary nature of the surviving resurrection narratives.
28:17: 17. "They worshipped him; but some doubted" — Alford argues this cannot mean some of the eleven doubted whether to worship Him (an absurd reading), and given the two prior Jerusalem appearances recorded in John 20, doubt among the apostles themselves at this point seems unlikely; he concludes others beyond the eleven — perhaps the "above five hundred brethren at once" of 1 Corinthians 15:6 — were probably present at this gathering, some of whom had not yet had opportunity to be convinced.
28:18: 18. "All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth" — Alford reads this as a direct echo of Daniel 7:14 (LXX), marking the Resurrection as the Father's sealing of the eternal covenant and Christ's exaltation as already accomplished and total, even before the Ascension's formal "taking possession of the inheritance."
28:19: 19. "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Alford insists on the force of μαθητεύσατε ("make disciples," not merely "teach" in the sense the English obscures) — the Lord's purpose is not to subdue the nations but to bring them, through instruction, into living discipleship. He defends the command as plainly addressed to the wider company of believers present, not the eleven alone (citing Acts 8:2, 4), and insists "all nations" includes, not excludes, the Jews — the temporary setting-aside of Israel consisting precisely in their now being numbered among "all the nations" rather than retaining a separate, privileged status. On baptism "into the name" (εἰς τὸ ὄνομα, not merely "in the name"), Alford stresses the single name (not "names") signifying the unity of the Godhead, and explains the formula as instituting the objective rite of Christian baptism, drawing a direct line back to Christ's own baptism, where all three Persons of the Trinity were manifest together. He firmly rejects any figurative or merely symbolic reading of the command as historically and textually untenable.
28:20: 20. "Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world (συντελείας τοῦ αἰῶνος)." Alford closes his commentary on Matthew by noting that this final clause founds the perpetual office of teaching and preaching in the Church, since the apostles living at that moment could not themselves teach all nations across all subsequent ages — the command and the promise together establishing an institution, not merely a single historical commission.
